stories.title: Why Can Birds Fly?
stories.text:
Guangguang lifts a tiny paper bird. "Why can real birds fly?"

Birds have light, hollow bones—less weight to lift.

Strong chest muscles pull those wings hard.

Feathers catch the air like soft little sails.

A flap pushes air down, and the bird goes up.

Gliding rides moving air under the curved wing.

People are heavier and have no wing feathers.

Airplanes borrow the same idea with big wings.

Watch how a wing curves when a bird turns.

Push, then coast. Push, then coast again.

Birds aren't magic—they're built for the sky.

Next time you see a bird, count one careful flap.

stories.title: Why Do Cats Purr?
stories.text:
A cat curls up. Rrr-rrr. Guangguang whispers, "Tiny motor?"

Cats often purr when they feel safe and happy.

Soft petting, resting, or snuggling can start the sound.

Muscles near the voice box vibrate as the cat breathes.

Air in, air out—tiny vibes make the purr.

Some cats also purr when they need comfort.

Nervous moments may bring a quiet, steady purr too.

Purring does not mean "leave me alone."

Soft ears and a soft body usually mean the cat likes it.

Pet gently. Watch the whole cat, not only the sound.

If the cat walks away, stop and give space.

Kind hands, calm purrs—friends who listen carefully.

stories.title: Why Do Dogs Wag Their Tails?
stories.text:
A dog's tail goes swish-swish. "Always happy?" asks Guangguang.

A wagging tail is a message, not just a yes.

A loose, wide wag with a soft body often means friendly joy.

A stiff, high wag can mean unsure or on alert.

Look at ears, mouth, and how close the dog stands.

The whole body tells the story of the wag.

Friendly excitement looks bouncy and soft.

Alert feelings look taller, tighter, and careful.

Never rush a dog you do not know.

Ask a grown-up before you say hello.

Friendly wags are nice—calm hands are kinder.

Read the dog. Then share a gentle hello.

stories.title: How Do Fish Breathe Underwater?
stories.text:
Guangguang peeks at a fish tank. "No trip up for air?"

Fish pull water in through their mouths.

Then they push water out over their gills.

Gills are thin layers that take oxygen from water.

Oxygen moves into the fish's blood—quiet and steady.

Gills work like tiny underwater lungs for water.

Clean water helps fish breathe easily.

If water has little oxygen, fish can struggle.

People breathe air with lungs.

Fish breathe oxygen dissolved in water.

Different tools, but the same need: oxygen.

Watch the tank. Thank the quiet gill work.

stories.title: Why Do Dogs Pant?
stories.text:
Warm day. A dog goes pant-pant. "Hot?" asks Guangguang.

Dogs do not sweat much through skin like people.

Panting moves air quickly over tongue and mouth.

That airflow helps heat leave the body.

After a run, panting is a dog's cooler.

Sunny days can bring long, easy pant-pant too.

Shade and water help a warm dog feel better.

If panting is very hard and the dog seems weak, get help.

Find shade, offer water, and tell a grown-up.

Never leave a dog in a hot car.

Rest and water help everyone cool down.

Pant means cool-down—care keeps dogs safe.

stories.title: Why Do Bees Make Honey?
stories.text:
A bee visits a flower. "Snack time?" asks Guangguang.

Bees collect sweet nectar from blossoms.

They carry it home to the hive in tiny belly tanks.

In the hive, bees pass nectar and fan their wings.

Fanning dries water out until nectar turns thick.

That thick golden food is honey for the colony.

Honey helps bees through cold or flower-scarce days.

While bees work, pollen sticks to their fuzzy bodies.

Pollen rides to other flowers and helps make seeds.

Honey is bee food first—people treat it carefully.

Watch bees from a safe distance with a grown-up.

Busy bees, sweet honey, and flowers that need friends.

stories.title: Why Are Some Animals Striped?
stories.text:
A zebra picture makes Guangguang tilt. "Fashion?"

Stripes can be more than decoration.

For a tiger in tall grass, stripes break up its shape.

Prey may not notice the outline as quickly.

For zebras in a group, many stripes can blur together.

A hunter may struggle to pick just one zebra.

Patterns match the places animals live and hide.

Spots, stripes, and colors can be survival tools.

Not every striped animal uses stripes the same way.

Science keeps learning from photos, tracks, and studies.

Next time you see stripes, ask: help or just pretty?

Patterns can be beautiful and useful at once.

stories.title: Why Did Dinosaurs Get So Big?
stories.text:
Guangguang holds a tiny toy T. rex. "School-bus big!"

Long ago, Earth had different plants and climates.

Some dinosaurs grew huge over many generations.

Big bodies can help reach high leaves for food.

Size can also help with defense in a wild world.

Growing big needs lots of food and time.

Not every dinosaur was a giant.

Many were chicken-sized or about dog-sized.

Fossils show bones, teeth, and footprints.

Scientists guess size and diet from those clues.

Movies exaggerate; fossils keep us honest.

Big or small, dinosaurs were real animals once.

stories.title: What Did T. rex Eat?
stories.text:
Guangguang shows long pointed teeth. "Salad?"

Tyrannosaurus rex had strong jaws and sharp teeth.

Those tools fit meat better than leafy salads.

It may have hunted living animals.

It may also have eaten animals already dead.

Big meat-eaters can do both kinds of feeding.

Tooth shape is a helpful clue.

Flat grinders often mean plant foods.

Sharp slicers often mean meat foods.

We learn from fossils, not movies alone.

T. rex was a powerful biter of its time.

Teeth tell stories if we look carefully.

stories.title: Why Do Whales Spout Water?
stories.text:
A whale blows a misty fountain. "Water fountain?"

Whales are mammals with lungs, not gills.

They must breathe air at the surface.

A blowhole sits on top of the head.

Warm breath whooshes out when the whale surfaces.

Cool air can turn that breath into mist.

The spout looks like water, but it is mostly breath cloud.

Then the whale breathes in and can dive again.

Different whales make different spout shapes.

Watch from a safe boat with grown-ups.

Kind watching keeps ocean friends safer.

Lungs, blowholes, and misty hellos at sea.

stories.title: Why Do Sharks Have So Many Teeth?
stories.text:
Guangguang counts cartoon shark teeth. "A hundred?"

Sharks grow many teeth in rows.

When a front tooth wears out, another can move up.

That keeps a working set for slippery food.

Lots of teeth means replaceable tools.

It does not mean a shark is "mean."

Different sharks eat different meals.

Some chase fish; some filter tiny plankton.

Healthy oceans help sharks and other sea life.

Respect wild sharks from a safe distance.

Teeth are tools that get replaced over time.

Ocean neighbors need clean, living seas.

stories.title: Why Do Camels Have Humps?
stories.text:
A camel hump looks like a backpack. "Water tank?"

A camel’s hump stores fat, not a jug of water.

Fat is energy when food is hard to find.

Deserts can be hot, dry, and scarce of snacks.

Camels also save water with clever bodies.

They handle heat and thirst better than many animals.

People once guessed humps were water bottles.

Science says: energy packs for the journey.

One-hump and two-hump camels both use fat stores.

After a hard trip, a soft hump can look leaner.

Food and rest help the energy pack refill.

Desert travelers with built-in snack backpacks.

stories.title: Why Do Owls Stay Up at Night?
stories.text:
An owl’s eyes look round and ready. "Night shift?"

Many owls hunt when nights are busy with small animals.

Mice and other snacks often move after dark.

Soft feathers help owls fly with quiet wings.

Big eyes gather dim moonlight and starlight.

Keen ears help find tiny rustling sounds.

Night tools fit night hunting.

Not every owl is strictly a night-only bird.

Some hunt at dawn or dusk too.

A hoot in the dark can mean a quiet flyer nearby.

Listen softly; give wild owls space.

Night-shift neighbors with silent wings.

stories.title: Why Do Butterflies Start as Caterpillars?
stories.text:
Guangguang peeks at a chrysalis. "Costume change?"

A butterfly's life starts as a tiny egg.

The egg hatches into a hungry little caterpillar.

The caterpillar eats leaves and grows very fast.

Then it makes a chrysalis—or soft pupa shell.

Inside the shell, the body quietly rebuilds.

Wings form. Legs change. A new shape waits.

At last, a butterfly climbs out carefully.

It waits for soft wings to dry and stiffen.

This big change is called metamorphosis.

Caterpillars and butterflies need different host plants.

A garden with the right leaves helps them thrive.

stories.title: Why Do Ants Walk in a Line?
stories.text:
Ants march in a neat line. "Parade?" asks Guangguang.

Ants leave scent trails for nest-mates to follow.

A good food find gets shared by the path they mark.

Other ants smell the trail and join the job.

Lines help many tiny workers move food efficiently.

Teamwork matters more than any one ant alone.

If a trail goes cold, ants may search new routes.

Their nest is a busy underground city of rooms.

Watch ants outdoors from a gentle distance.

Do not poke nests—ants need calm space to work.

Little insects show big cooperation every day.

Follow the scent road: science in tiny steps.

stories.title: Why Do Sea Turtles Come Ashore?
stories.text:
A turtle crawls onto sand. "Beach day?"

Many sea turtles lay eggs on sandy beaches.

They grew in the ocean but need land for nests.

A mother digs a soft pit above the tide line.

She lays eggs, covers them, then returns to sea.

Warm sand helps the eggs develop over time.

Hatchlings later race toward the bright ocean.

Lights and trash on beaches can confuse them.

Kind people keep nesting beaches dark and clean.

Never pick up wild hatchlings without experts.

Ocean homes, sandy nurseries, careful humans.

Sand, eggs, and a long swim ahead.

stories.title: Why Do Frogs Jump So Far?
stories.text:
A frog leaps. Boing! "Super legs?"

Frog back legs are long and strong.

Muscles store a springy push for takeoff.

Webbed feet help landings and swimming too.

Jumping helps frogs catch food and escape danger.

Not every hop is the same length.

Some frogs climb; some swim more than they leap.

Look at the whole frog, not only the jump.

Wet skin needs moist places to stay healthy.

Ponds and clean water help frog neighbors.

Strong legs, soft landings, careful habitats.

Boing science: push, fly, splash.

stories.title: Why Do Octopuses Have Eight Arms?
stories.text:
An octopus waves many arms. "Why eight?"

Eight arms help grab, taste, and explore.

Suckers can hold rocks, food, and tools.

Arms let an octopus open shells cleverly.

They also help crawl across the seafloor.

An octopus can squeeze through small gaps.

Soft bodies plus many arms make great explorers.

Ink and color changes help them stay safe.

Ocean rocks and reefs are favorite hideouts.

Watch gently in aquariums with grown-ups.

Eight helpers for a curious ocean mind.

Grab, taste, hide, explore.

stories.title: Why Do Penguins Huddle Together?
stories.text:
Penguins pack into a fluffy crowd. "Group hug?"

Cold winds steal heat from lonely birds.

A huddle shares warmth across many bodies.

Penguins take turns at the chilly outer edge.

Friends in the middle get a warmer break.

Huddles help eggs and chicks stay safer too.

Teamwork is survival on icy shores.

Not every penguin species huddles the same way.

Watching from afar keeps wild birds calm.

Warmth, turns, and togetherness matter here.

Cold places reward good neighbors.

Fluffy science: share the heat.

stories.title: Why Do Elephants Have Trunks?
stories.text:
An elephant trunk swings. "Super nose?"

A trunk is a nose and a helper hand together.

Elephants smell, breathe, and drink with it.

They can grab leaves and lift light objects.

Trunks spray water for cool baths.

Soft tip fingers help careful picking.

Babies practice trunk skills as they grow.

Herds use trunks in gentle hellos too.

Never tease wild elephants—give wide space.

Respect big animals with quiet watching.

Nose plus hand equals trunk power.

Smell, sip, spray, say hello.

stories.title: Why Do Giraffes Have Long Necks?
stories.text:
A giraffe stretches high. "Why so tall?"

Long necks help reach leaves other animals miss.

Tall browsing can mean extra food options.

Necks also help giraffes watch for danger far away.

Strong hearts pump blood up that long path.

Special valves help blood flow carefully.

Calves grow into their height over time.

Not every tall animal uses height the same way.

Savanna trees and giraffes fit together.

Watch quietly; wild giraffes need calm space.

High snacks, far views, careful bodies.

Tall science under the sun.

stories.title: Why Do Spiders Spin Webs?
stories.text:
A shiny web sparkles. "Art project?"

Many spiders spin silk from their bodies.

Webs can catch flying insects for food.

Different web shapes fit different hunting styles.

Silk is strong for its thin size.

Spiders may rebuild webs when weather tears them.

Not every spider waits on a big orb web.

Some hunt by chasing or hiding instead.

Most spiders are helpful neighbors for gardens.

Give them space; watch without touching webs.

Silk threads, patient hunters, tiny engineers.

Sparkle science between leaves.

stories.title: Why Do Bats Sleep Upside Down?
stories.text:
Guangguang hangs a sock by its toes. "Bats sleep upside down—why?"

Bat feet lock around a perch so hanging takes little energy.

Their legs and hips are built for dangling, not long walking.

From a hang, a bat can drop and open wings into flight fast.

Taking off from the ground is harder for many bat bodies.

Caves, trees, and quiet roofs make safe upside-down bedrooms.

Hanging high keeps bats away from many ground hunters.

They rest by day and wake to hunt insects in soft night air.

Echolocation clicks help some bats find food in the dark.

Bats are helpers: many eat mosquitoes and other pests.

Watch bats from a calm distance—never poke roosts.

Toes lock, drop, and fly: a clever upside-down bedtime.

stories.title: Why Do Zebras Have Stripes?
stories.text:
Black and white flash by. "Why stripes?" asks Guangguang.

Scientists study several helpful stripe ideas together.

Stripes may confuse biting flies that chase solid shapes.

Moving stripes can make it harder for flies to land.

In a herd, stripes may blur who begins and who ends.

That blur can make a hunter pause for a moment.

Stripes also help zebras recognize family patterns.

Each zebra's stripe map is a little different.

Open grasslands are bright—patterns matter in motion.

Zebras still need space, water, and calm watching.

Never chase wild zebras; learn from books and zoos too.

Stripes: fly tips, herd blur, and family ID—science keeps asking.

stories.title: Why Do Kangaroos Hop?
stories.text:
Guangguang bounce-bounces. "Why hop?"

Kangaroos have strong back legs and long springy feet.

Hopping stores and returns energy like a soft pogo.

Tendons stretch and snap back to help the next jump.

At travel speed, hopping can save energy on open land.

A heavy tail helps balance like a friendly third leg.

Front paws are free for soft touches and little tasks.

Joeys ride in a pouch while moms hop carefully.

Different kangaroo sizes hop in their own ways.

Give wild hoppers wide space—no chasing for fun.

Watch with a grown-up and cheer from far away.

Strong legs, spring tendons, balanced tail: hop science.

stories.title: Why Do Dolphins Click and Whistle?
stories.text:
Clicks echo in Guangguang's pretend ocean. "Why so noisy?"

Dolphins use sound to talk with friends nearby.

Whistles can be like names that help them find each other.

Clicks bounce off fish and return as soft echo maps.

That echo sense is called echolocation—seeing with sound.

Murky water is less of a problem when ears lead the way.

Pods stay close by chatting across short distances.

Playful leaps and spins often come with happy sounds.

Listening quietly teaches more than chasing boats.

Wild dolphins need calm seas and respectful space.

Learn from aquariums and nature shows with a grown-up.

Click, whistle, listen: ocean friends speak in sound.

stories.title: Why Do Fireflies Glow?
stories.text:
Tiny lights blink in the grass. "Why glow?"

Fireflies make light with a gentle chemical reaction.

The glow is cold light—little heat, lots of soft shine.

Different blink patterns help fireflies find partners.

Some patterns say hello; others say this spot is mine.

Larvae may glow too as they grow toward flashy nights.

Warm evenings after rain often bring more blinks.

City lights can hide the tiny messages—dark helps.

Cupping a firefly briefly then letting it go is kind.

Never spray chemicals where soft blinkers live.

Sit still and count flashes like a night science game.

Chemistry, patterns, and patience: backyard star bugs.

stories.title: Why Do Crabs Walk Sideways?
stories.text:
A crab skitters left. "Why sideways?" Guangguang laughs.

Many crab leg joints swing best in a side-to-side path.

Side steps fit their wide flat bodies on sand and rock.

Quick sideways dashes help them slip into tiny shelters.

Some crabs can walk forward a little, but side is smoother.

Claws up front are busy—legs behind do the travel work.

Tide pools are busy cities of sideways traffic.

Watch footprints in wet sand: little side-dash tracks.

Give crabs room; pinching claws are for crab business.

Never yank a crab from a rock hole—it needs that home.

Tide pool rules: look, learn, leave creatures in place.

Sideways isn't silly—it's joint design on the move.

stories.title: Why Do Beavers Build Dams?
stories.text:
Splash! Sticks pile up. "Why build dams?"

Beavers cut trees and pack mud to slow a stream.

The pond behind a dam makes a safer deep home zone.

Deep water hides the entrance to their lodge.

Stored branches underwater are winter snack shelves.

Dam ponds also help other animals find wet habitat.

Engineers with orange teeth reshaping the creek.

Listen for soft slap warnings on the water surface.

Leave beaver work alone—removing dams can harm homes.

Watch from a trail with a grown-up and binoculars.

Nature's builders teach patience and planning.

Stick, mud, pond, lodge: beaver town planning.

stories.title: Why Do Snakes Stick Out Their Tongues?
stories.text:
A tongue flicks softly. "Why?" asks Guangguang kindly.

Snakes smell with their tongues—not to be rude.

Tiny scent bits stick to the tongue tip.

The tongue carries smells to a special nose-inside sensor.

That sensor helps map where prey or paths might be.

Flicking gathers fresh air samples again and again.

A forked tip can compare left and right scent clues.

Snakes are shy neighbors; most want quiet space.

Never grab or tease a snake—call a grown-up if worried.

Learn safe local snakes from park rangers and books.

Curiosity is good; touching wild snakes is not.

Flick, sense, map: tongues that smell the world.

stories.title: Why Do Hummingbirds Hover?
stories.text:
Wings blur. "How do they hang in the air?" Guangguang asks.

Hummingbirds beat their wings in a special figure-eight path.

That path makes lift on both the forward and back strokes.

Most birds get lift mainly on the downstroke—hover needs both.

Tiny strong muscles power hundreds of beats each second.

Hovering lets them sip nectar while staying at the flower.

They can also fly backward and sideways for careful sips.

High-energy food from flowers fuels the busy wing work.

Garden feeders help when placed clean and high enough.

Watch softly—sudden moves can scare these tiny flyers.

Never grab a hummingbird; eyes and quiet feet are enough.

Figure-eight wings + fuel = floating flower visits.

stories.title: Why Do Polar Bears Have White Fur?
stories.text:
White fur against snow. "Camouflage?" Max asks.

Polar bear fur looks white, which helps them blend on ice.

Each hair is mostly clear and hollow like a soft tube.

Light scatters in the hollow hairs so we see white.

Under the fur, skin is dark and helps hold warmth.

Fat and fur coats keep heat in freezing winds.

Big paws spread weight on snow like soft snowshoes.

Hunting needs patience; white helps them stay less noticed.

Climate and ice changes matter a lot for their homes.

Learn and care—wild bears need distant respect always.

Never approach a polar bear; watch films and museums instead.

Hollow hairs, dark skin, thick coats: Arctic design.

stories.title: Why Is Grass Green?
stories.text:
Lawn picnic. "Why green, not purple?"

Grass leaves hold a tiny helper called chlorophyll.

Chlorophyll catches sunlight to help make food.

It reflects more green light toward our eyes.

So grass looks green while it works.

Other paints in leaves hide under that green.

In fall, some greens fade and reds show up.

Healthy grass still needs water and light.

Too little sun can make grass look pale.

Green is a working color, not just decoration.

Touch soft blades—tiny solar kitchens.

Green grass means sunlight helpers are busy!

stories.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
stories.text:
Pretend sip—blech! "Why so salty?"

Rain falls on rocks and soil inland.

Water picks up tiny mineral bits, including salt.

Rivers carry those bits toward the sea.

Ocean water keeps collecting dissolved minerals.

Sun evaporates water, but salt mostly stays behind.

Over long time, seas taste salty.

Not every lake is as salty as the ocean.

Some inland seas can be even saltier.

Salt is a traveler that settled in the big blue.

Waves splash—taste is science, not magic.

Rinse hands after beach play—salt sticks!

stories.title: Why Do Onions Make Us Cry?
stories.text:
Chop chop—then sniffles. Onion tears!

Cutting an onion breaks open tiny cells.

Those cells release sharp-smelling gases.

The gases rise and tickle your eyes.

Eyes make tears to wash the tickle away.

Tears are a helpful rinse, not sadness only.

Chilling an onion can slow the gas a bit.

Cut near a gentle fan blowing gases away.

Grown-ups may cry too—same onion chemistry.

Soup still tastes great after the sniffles.

Science in the kitchen: smell meeting eyes.

Blink, smile, keep cooking with care.

stories.title: Why Does Popcorn Pop?
stories.text:
A quiet kernel sits still on the counter. Then—POP!

Guangguang jumps. "Why does popcorn pop like that?"

Inside each hard kernel is a little water.

Heat turns that tiny water into steam.

Steam needs more room than liquid water.

Pressure builds inside the tough little shell.

Suddenly the hard shell bursts wide open.

The soft inside flips out fluffy and white.

That's the loud pop you hear and see.

If a kernel is too dry, it may not pop.

Heat and a sip of water work as a team.

Not exploding candy—just a steamy seed surprise.

stories.title: Why Do Magnets Stick to Some Things?
stories.text:
Fridge magnet sticks. "Why not wood?"

Magnets pull on iron, nickel, and some steels.

Those metals have tiny magnetic regions inside.

A magnet can line them up and hold on.

Wood, plastic, and glass usually do not stick.

They lack those ready magnetic partners.

Two magnet poles can attract or push apart.

Opposite poles pull together; same poles push.

Magnet power fades with distance.

Compasses use Earth's big magnetic field.

Stick science is selective—not magic glue.

Try fridge, keys, and a wooden spoon—compare!

stories.title: Why Do Bananas Turn Brown?
stories.text:
A yellow banana gets freckles, then brown. "Why?" asks Guangguang.

Bananas keep changing after they are picked.

A natural signal tells them it is time to ripen.

Soft enzymes break down the firm parts inside.

The peel’s yellow color slowly gives way to brown spots.

Sweeter soft fruit is easier for animals—and kids—to enjoy.

Cooler storage slows the browning; warm kitchens speed it up.

Brown freckles can mean ripe and ready, not always “bad.”

If it smells off or is mushy-weird, ask a grown-up before eating.

Browning is ripening chemistry wearing freckles.

Make banana bread with a grown-up when spots arrive.

Ripen, soften, freckle: banana science.

stories.title: Why Does Metal Feel Colder Than Wood?
stories.text:
Guangguang touches a metal spoon and a wooden spoon. "Metal feels colder—same room?"

Often both spoons are nearly the same temperature in the room.

Metal moves heat away from your fingers quickly.

That fast heat steal makes metal feel colder to the touch.

Wood holds heat closer and moves it more slowly.

So wood can feel warmer even when the thermometer agrees.

Tile floors and metal doorknobs play the same trick.

Your skin is a heat detective, not always a temperature label.

Scientists call the quick heat-moving ability conductivity.

Feeling cold can mean heat leaving you fast.

Touch both spoons with a grown-up and compare the surprise.

Heat flows fast in metal: touch science.

stories.title: Why Do We Hiccup?
stories.text:
Hic—! Guangguang blinks. "Why do we hiccup?"

A hiccup is a sudden squeeze of the diaphragm under your lungs.

Air pops in quickly when that muscle jumps.

Your voice box makes a tiny “hic” sound.

Spicy food, giggles, or gulping air can wake the hiccups.

Most hiccup spells stop on their own after a little while.

Slow breaths and a calm sip of water often help.

Hiccups are annoying, not usually a big danger.

If they last a very long time, tell a grown-up.

A hiccup is a surprise squeeze concert in your chest.

Giggle about it—then breathe soft like a sleepy kitten.

Diaphragm jump: hiccup science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Five Fingers?
stories.text:
Guangguang counts fingers. "Why five?"

Humans usually grow five digits on each hand.

That layout helps us grip, pinch, and use tools.

Thumbs that can touch other fingers make fine work easier.

Fossils show distant relatives also had a five-digit pattern.

Not every animal matches our count—horses and birds differ.

Five is common for us, not a magic perfect number for all life.

Hands learn skills with practice: writing, tying, catching.

Keep fingers safe from doors and sharp tools with care.

Five fingers are a handy toolkit grown on your palms.

Trace your hand and label each helper finger with a grown-up.

Grip, pinch, tool use: five-finger science.

stories.title: Why Does Bread Get Moldy?
stories.text:
Green fuzz on bread. "Ew—why?" asks Guangguang.

Mold is a tiny living fungus, not magic dirt.

Spores float in air and can land on food.

They grow when bread is moist and not too cold.

Bread is a cozy buffet of starch for them.

Cool, dry, sealed storage slows the fuzzy party.

Seeing mold means skip that slice—don’t just scrape.

Ask a grown-up before tossing or saving nearby pieces.

Some cheeses use friendly molds on purpose; sandwich bread usually does not.

Moldy bread is fungus having a picnic.

Check the bag date and keep the loaf closed tight.

Spores, moisture, buffet: mold science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Eyebrows?
stories.text:
Guangguang draws brows on a face. "What for?"

Eyebrows help keep sweat and rain from running into your eyes.

They act like tiny umbrellas above your gaze.

Brows also show feelings—surprise, worry, joy.

Friends can read your face partly by watching them move.

Without brows, expressions can look flatter.

Hair there grows in a special shape on the brow bone.

Gently patting sweat away still helps on hot days.

Never shave experiments without a grown-up’s okay.

Eyebrows are rain guards and feeling flags together.

Make silly brow faces in a mirror and laugh.

Shield plus signal: eyebrow science.

stories.title: Why Does Ice Cream Melt?
stories.text:
A scoop sags. "Why so fast?" Max wails.

Ice cream is frozen water, fat, and sugar mixed with air.

Warm air and your tongue add heat to the scoop.

Heat makes ice crystals turn back into liquid.

That is why the scoop collapses into a sweet puddle.

Shade and a cold bowl slow the melt; sun speeds it up.

Licking fast is a race against soft physics.

Dropped scoops on hot sidewalks melt even quicker.

Freezers keep crystals solid until snack time.

Melting is heat winning a gentle tug-of-war with ice.

Eat outside with a grown-up’s napkin plan ready.

Heat vs ice crystals: melt science.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Hiccups After Soda?
stories.text:
Fizz! Hic! "Why now?" asks Guangguang.

Bubbly drinks can tickle your stomach.

They can also bother the diaphragm under your lungs.

A sudden squeeze makes that tiny “hic.”

Cold fizz and fast gulps make hiccups more likely.

Slow sips give your body a calmer chance.

Most soda hiccups fade after a short wait.

A quiet breath and a water sip may help settle things.

You did nothing “wrong”—bubbles just woke a reflex.

Fizz plus diaphragm equals a surprise hic concert.

Pause between gulps when drinks are very bubbly.

Bubbles tickle, then hic: soda-hiccup science.

stories.title: Why Is Honey Sticky?
stories.text:
Honey clings to Guangguang’s spoon. "Why so sticky?"

Honey is mostly sugars dissolved in a tiny bit of water.

Those sugar chains grab onto each other and onto the spoon.

Thick liquids flow slowly; scientists call that viscosity.

Bees remove a lot of water so honey stays thick and lasting.

Warmth makes honey runnier; cool makes it cling more.

A little honey on toast can drip in slow golden ribbons.

Sticky is useful: it stays put for bees and for snacks.

Wash sticky fingers with warm water—sugar loves water.

Stickiness is sugar chemistry holding hands.

Taste a tiny drop with a grown-up and feel the cling.

Golden cling: honey science.

stories.title: Why Do We Dream?
stories.text:
Max wakes from a funny dream. "Guangguang, why do we dream?"

While you sleep, your brain stays busy sorting the day.

Dreams can mix memories, feelings, and little made-up scenes.

Some dreams feel like practice for feelings or ideas.

REM sleep is a stage when dreams often get vivid.

Not every dream has a secret code—many are brain play.

Scary dreams can fade if you tell a grown-up and breathe.

Good sleep habits help the brain’s night cleanup.

Dreams do not predict the future like a crystal ball.

Night stories are your brain’s soft rehearsal room.

Keep a tiny dream notebook if you like remembering.

Sleep, sort, dream: brain night science.

stories.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
stories.text:
The moon looks skinny tonight. "Did it shrink?" asks Guangguang.

The moon is still round; we only see lit parts change.

Sunlight hits half the moon like a lamp on a ball.

As the moon orbits Earth, our view of the lit half shifts.

New moon hides the lit face from us; full moon shows it.

Crescents and halves are just different viewing angles.

The moon does not make its own bright light—it reflects.

Phases repeat in a gentle monthly cycle.

Clouds can hide the moon, but the phase still continues.

Changing shape is changing shadow-and-light view.

Watch the sky a week and notice the slow shift.

Orbit, light, phase: moon science.

stories.title: Why Do Apples Turn Brown After Cutting?
stories.text:
A cut apple turns brown. "Is it spoiled already?" asks Max.

Cutting lets air meet the apple’s inside chemicals.

An enzyme starts a browning reaction with oxygen.

Brown is a color change, not always a danger sign.

Lemon juice or chill can slow the browning.

Whole uncut apples stay protected by their peel.

Browning apples can still taste fine for a while.

If it smells weird or feels slimy, ask a grown-up.

Cooks use browning tricks in pies and snacks.

Cut + air + enzyme = freckle chemistry.

Try lemon on half a slice with a grown-up.

Apple freckles: cut-fruit science.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Two Eyes?
stories.text:
Mia covers one eye. "Why two eyes, Guangguang?"

Each eye sees a slightly different picture.

Your brain blends both views into one smart scene.

Two views help you judge near and far—depth.

Catching a ball or pouring juice uses depth cues.

One eye still sees a lot; two eyes add 3D help.

Animals use eyes in different places for their lives.

Glasses and checkups keep both eyes working kindly.

Closing one eye makes stacking blocks trickier.

Two cameras, one brain movie.

Try the cover-one-eye game with a grown-up.

Depth duo: eye science.

stories.title: Why Does Salt Melt Ice on Sidewalks?
stories.text:
Salt on icy steps. "How does salt melt ice?" asks Max.

Ice likes a certain freezing temperature.

Salt mixes with the thin water film on ice.

That mix freezes at a lower temperature than plain water.

So ice can melt even when air is still chilly.

Workers sprinkle salt to make walkways safer.

Too much salt can bother plants—use carefully.

Sand can add grip without melting as much.

Warm sun and salt often team up on sidewalks.

Lower freeze point = melt help.

Watch salt work on a tiny ice cube with a grown-up.

Sidewalk thaw: salt science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Belly Buttons?
stories.text:
Mia peeks at her belly button. "Why is this here?"

Before birth, a cord brought food and oxygen from Mom.

That cord connected at the place that becomes your navel.

After birth, the cord is gently clamped and falls away.

The soft mark left behind is your belly button.

Innies and outies are just different healing shapes.

Everyone who grew with a cord has a navel story.

Keep it clean like the rest of your tummy skin.

It is a tiny scar of how you were fed early on.

Your first delivery door—closed for good.

Ask a grown-up about baby photos of the cord stump.

Navel note: body beginning science.

stories.title: Why Do Balloons Stick to Hair After Rubbing?
stories.text:
A rubbed balloon sticks to Max’s hair. "Magic?" laughs Guangguang.

Rubbing moves tiny charges between balloon and hair.

Opposite charges attract—so hair and balloon cling.

Scientists call this static electricity.

Dry air makes static tricks show up more often.

The balloon can also stick lightly to a wall.

Touching metal can quietly share charges away.

Static is not lightning, but both involve charge.

Hair standing up is charges pushing alike apart.

Rub, charge, cling: soft electric play.

Try the balloon-on-wall test with a grown-up.

Static cling: balloon science.

stories.title: Why Do Leaves Fall in Autumn?
stories.text:
Orange leaves drift down. "Why fall now?" asks Guangguang.

Trees sense shorter days and cooler air.

They seal tiny doorways at each leaf stem.

Chlorophyll fades; other colors shine through.

Falling leaves help trees rest through winter.

On the ground, leaves become soft soil food.

Evergreens keep needles with special wax coats.

Wind is a helper, not the only reason leaves drop.

Raking can be a gentle outdoor chore with grown-ups.

Autumn is a planned goodbye, not a broken tree.

Catch one leaf and notice its stem scar.

Seal, color, fall: leaf science.

stories.title: Why Does Pepper Make You Sneeze?
stories.text:
Pepper dust makes Max achoo. "Why sneeze?" asks Guangguang.

Tiny pepper bits tickle sensors in your nose.

Nerves send a fast message: clear this out!

A sneeze blasts air to push the tickle away.

Eyes may water a little from the same reflex path.

Pepper is not germs—just a spicy dust alarm.

Covering a sneeze keeps droplets kinder to friends.

A tissue or elbow is a polite sneeze shield.

Cooking with a grown-up? Keep pepper jars calm.

Tickle → signal → blast: sneeze science.

Smell gentle spices from a safe distance.

Achoo alarm: nose science.

stories.title: Why Is Fire Hot?
stories.text:
A candle glows. "Why is fire hot?" whispers Guangguang.

Fire is a fast chemical dance with fuel and oxygen.

That dance releases energy we feel as heat and see as light.

Different fuels burn at different warmth levels.

Grown-ups keep flames in safe places like candles or stoves.

Never touch fire or play with matches—ask for help.

Smoke means leftover bits floating away; step back.

Firefighters train to cool and stop unsafe fires.

Heat can cook food when adults control it carefully.

Hot means energy pouring out of the reaction.

Watch a candle only with a grown-up nearby.

Fuel, air, heat: fire science—safely.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Brain Freeze From Cold Drinks?
stories.text:
Icy slush makes Max wince. "Brain freeze!"

Cold touches the roof of your mouth suddenly.

Blood vessels there tighten, then open quickly.

Nerves near your forehead feel the change as a sharp ache.

It is not your brain turning into ice.

Slow sips warm the mouth and calm the signal.

Pressing your tongue to the roof can help gently.

Warmth returns; the freeze usually fades fast.

Treats are fun—just go a little slower.

Cold shock → vessel dance → brief ouch.

Share a slush with a grown-up at easy speed.

Slush pause: cold-drink science.

stories.title: Why Do Cats Knead Soft Blankets?
stories.text:
A cat presses paws on a blanket. "Why knead?" asks Mia.

Kitten kneading helped milk flow from Mom.

Grown cats keep the cozy habit when happy.

Soft blankets feel like a safe nest spot.

Kneading can release a little calming scent from paws.

It is affection, not scratching to be mean.

If claws prick, a soft pad or thick blanket helps.

Different cats knead more or less—personalities differ.

Pet gently when the cat invites you.

Paw press = comfort memory.

Watch your cat’s soft rhythm with a grown-up.

Knead joy: cat science.

stories.title: Why Does Metal Rust?
stories.text:
An old bike shows orange flakes. "What is rust?"

Iron in metal meets water and air oxygen.

They slowly make a new crumbly orange material.

Rust is a chemical change, not dirt you wipe once.

Paint and oil can slow water from reaching metal.

Stainless mixes help resist rust better.

Wet bikes left outside rust faster.

Gentle drying after rain is a kind habit.

Ask a grown-up before scrubbing rusty tools.

Iron + water + air = slow orange change.

Wipe a wet bike chain together carefully.

Rust watch: metal science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Different Blood Types?
stories.text:
Mia hears “blood type.” "Why different kinds?"

Tiny markers on blood cells come in a few letter teams.

A, B, AB, and O are common type names kids may hear.

Your type is inherited from family patterns.

Doctors match types carefully for transfusions.

Having a type is normal—not a contest or rank.

Only medical people should handle blood tests.

Eating veggies and resting help your whole body.

Curiosity is fine; needles belong to clinics.

Markers differ; blood still carries life jobs.

Ask a grown-up what your family knows gently.

Type tags: body science.

stories.title: Why Do Stars Look Pointy in Drawings?
stories.text:
Max draws a star with spikes. "Are stars pointy?"

Real stars are giant glowing balls of gas.

From Earth they look like tiny dots of light.

Our eyes and air make sparkles that feel spiky.

Artists draw points to show that sparkle feeling.

Cameras can catch spikes from lens tricks too.

Telescopes show rounder discs of bright stars.

Constellation stick-figures are helpful maps, not wires.

Night drawings can be science plus imagination.

Pointy is a symbol for twinkle.

Compare a drawing to a real sky with a grown-up.

Twinkle art: star science.

stories.title: Why Do We Yawn When Others Yawn?
stories.text:
Mia yawns after Guangguang yawns. "Contagious?"

Seeing or hearing a yawn can nudge your brain to copy.

Scientists think it links to empathy and group sync.

Your body may also need a stretch of jaw and air.

Yawning can happen when you are tired or bored.

Copying is not rude—it is a social echo.

Animals yawn too; some species share the echo.

A polite cover of the mouth is kind manners.

Fresh air and sleep help real tiredness.

Echo yawn = brain noticing friends.

Try noticing who yawns first in a cozy room.

Yawn echo: people science.

stories.title: Why Does Glue Stick?
stories.text:
Glue holds paper. "How does sticky work?" asks Max.

Wet glue flows into tiny bumps on surfaces.

As it dries, it hardens and locks those bumps.

Some glues make chemical bonds with the material.

Different glues fit paper, wood, or fabric jobs.

Too much glue can stay soft and fail.

Clean, dry surfaces help glue grab better.

Use school glue with a grown-up’s rules.

Fingers sticky? Warm water and soap help.

Flow, dry, lock: stick science.

Make a tiny paper sandwich test together.

Hold tight: glue science.

stories.title: Why Do We See Our Breath in Winter?
stories.text:
Mia puffs a cloud outside. "Is that smoke?"

Your breath carries warm water vapor from inside.

Cold air cools that vapor into tiny droplets.

The cloud is a mini fog of water, not fire smoke.

Warmer rooms hide the cloud because air stays softer.

On frosty days the contrast makes clouds pop.

Animals make breath clouds too in winter.

Scarves can catch moisture—keep them dry and cozy.

Breath clouds vanish as droplets spread out.

Warm wet air + cold = visible puff.

Make gentle puffs with a grown-up outdoors.

Winter puff: breath science.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Sleep?
stories.text:
Guangguang yawns wide. "Nap attack!"

Sleep lets your body and brain recover.

While you rest, your brain sorts memories.

Your body repairs tiny wear and grows.

Kids need plenty of sleep—growing is busy work.

Dim lights tell your brain night is near.

Quiet stories help the body slow down.

Bright screens late can keep you too alert.

A calm bedtime is like a soft off-switch.

Sleep is not wasted time—it is nightly repair.

Rest well, then wake ready to play and learn.

Goodnight, little repair crew inside you.

stories.title: Why Do We Yawn?
stories.text:
A big yawn spreads. Contagious!

Scientists still study why we yawn.

It may help cool a warm busy brain.

A yawn can wake you a little bit.

It can also signal rest time to friends.

Seeing a yawn often makes you yawn too.

Humans copy soft signals—we are social.

Yawning does not always mean you are bored.

Sometimes your body wants a quick reset.

Stretch, breathe, and follow a night yawn to bed.

Day yawns can mean you need a short break.

Smile—your body just asked for a tiny reset.

stories.title: Why Do We Blink?
stories.text:
Guangguang tries not to blink. Impossible!

Your eyelids close and open—blink, blink.

Each blink spreads tears like a tiny wipe.

Tears wash away dust so eyes stay clear.

Moist eyes feel soft and comfortable.

Most blinks happen without you thinking.

Screens can make us blink less often.

Fewer blinks mean eyes feel dry and tired.

Soft, slow blinks help the surface shine.

Look far away for a gentle eye break.

Your eyelids are tiny windshield wipers.

Blink kindly—then your eyes say thank you.

stories.title: Why Does My Heart Beat?
stories.text:
Hand on chest: thump-thump. "A drum?"

Your heart is a strong muscle pump.

It pushes blood through soft tube paths.

Those paths are called blood vessels.

Blood carries oxygen and food to you.

Then blood returns to refill oxygen from lungs.

Exercise makes the heart beat faster.

Your body asks for more delivery right then.

Rest slows the beat to a calm rhythm.

A steady heartbeat is your delivery system.

Feel your pulse—gentle drum for life.

Thank your heart for every quiet thump.

stories.title: Why Do I Get a Fever?
stories.text:
Cheeks feel warm. "Broken thermostat?"

A fever often means your body is fighting germs.

A little higher heat can help defenses work.

Your immune team works hard when you feel hot.

Fevers can have other causes too.

Grown-ups decide what care you need.

Rest helps your body use its energy wisely.

Sips of water or warm drinks help a lot.

Medicine is only from a trusted adult.

Never grab pills by yourself.

Fever is a signal, not a game.

Ask for help, rest, and feel the care.

stories.title: Why Do We Wash Hands with Soap?
stories.text:
Sink time! "Why soap, not only water?" asks Guangguang.

Hands pick up tiny germs from doors, toys, and snacks.

Water alone rinses some dirt but misses oily spots.

Soap grabs oils and lifts germs so water can rinse them away.

Bubbles help soap reach cracks around nails and fingers.

Twenty seconds of scrubbing covers fronts, backs, and thumbs.

Sing a short song while you scrub to mark the time.

Rinse well, then dry—damp hands grab new germs faster.

Wash before eating and after bathroom or pet play.

Soap is a helper tool, not a scary chemical fight.

Clean hands protect you and the people you hug.

Soap + scrub + rinse + dry: tiny everyday science.

stories.title: Why Do Baby Teeth Fall Out?
stories.text:
A tooth wiggles. "Is it broken?" Guangguang worries.

Baby teeth are starters that fit a smaller jaw.

As you grow, adult teeth push up from underneath.

Roots of baby teeth shrink so the tooth can loosen.

Wiggling is often a sign the new tooth is ready.

Losing teeth makes room for bigger chewing tools.

Most kids lose teeth over several years, not all at once.

Gentle brushing still matters for wiggly and new teeth.

Do not yank hard—let the tooth leave when ready.

If a tooth hurts a lot, ask a grown-up or dentist.

A new smile grows one careful tooth at a time.

Small starters make way for grown-up chewers.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Goosebumps?
stories.text:
Arms prickle. "Tiny bumps—why?" asks Guangguang.

Goosebumps happen when tiny muscles at hair roots tighten.

Cold can trigger the bumps to try to trap a little warmth.

Long ago, fluffier fur would have puffed up more.

People have thinner hair, so bumps look small now.

Big feelings—awe, scare, music—can also flip the switch.

Your body shares an old alert system with other animals.

A sweater or warm hug often smooths cold bumps away.

Scary movies can raise bumps even when you are safe.

Bumps are a signal, not a sickness by themselves.

Notice them, get cozy, and breathe if feelings feel big.

Tiny muscles, old fur trick, modern soft reminders.

stories.title: Why Do We Sneeze?
stories.text:
Ah—choo! "Why sneeze?" Guangguang asks after a tissue.

A sneeze is a fast blast that clears the nose path.

Dust, pollen, or a tickle can wake sneeze sensors.

Your body pushes air out to sweep the irritant away.

Eyes may close for a blink during the big blast.

Covering with a tissue or elbow keeps spray kinder.

Some sneezes come with colds; some are just dust.

Bright light makes a few people sneeze—a curious quirk.

If sneezes keep coming, a grown-up can help check why.

Hydration and clean air can calm a tickly nose.

Sneezes are helpers, even when they interrupt stories.

Sensors, blast, cover: nose cleanup in a flash.

stories.title: Why Do I Have a Belly Button?
stories.text:
Shirt up. "This button does nothing—why keep it?"

Before birth, a cord brought food and oxygen to you.

That cord connected to the place that is now your navel.

After birth the cord is clamped and gently falls away.

The healed spot becomes your belly button scar-soft mark.

Innies and outies are both normal shapes of healing.

The button is a reminder of how you grew, not a toy.

Keep it clean like the rest of your skin in the bath.

Doctors checked it when you were a tiny newborn.

Every person who grew that way has a belly button story.

It is quiet history written on your middle.

Cord, heal, mark: your first delivery line.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Skin?
stories.text:
"Skin is just wrapping—right?" Guangguang taps softly.

Skin is a living shield that keeps insides safely in.

It blocks many germs and dirt from easy entry.

Skin helps hold moisture so you do not dry out.

Nerves in skin tell you hot, cold, soft, and ouch.

Sweat glands help cool you when you run and play.

Melanin pigment gives a range of beautiful skin tones.

Cuts trigger a repair team of clotting and new cells.

Gentle washing and lotion keep the shield comfortable.

Sunscreen and shade protect skin on bright days.

Your largest organ works quietly every minute.

Shield, sense, cool, heal: skin does big jobs.

stories.title: Why Do Muscles Get Sore After Exercise?
stories.text:
Stairs hurt tomorrow. "Did I break my legs?"

Hard play makes tiny muscle fiber repairs begin.

Soreness often peaks a day later as rebuilding starts.

Your body reinforces muscles so next time feels easier.

This delayed ache is common after new or big efforts.

Gentle movement, water, and sleep help recovery.

Stretching softly can feel nice but is not magic alone.

Sharp sudden pain is different—tell a grown-up then.

Rest days let the rebuild finish its quiet work.

Stronger muscles are a gift from careful practice.

Soreness means remodel, not that you failed.

Work, tiny repair, stronger: workout science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Two Kidneys?
stories.text:
"Two filters—why not one?" Guangguang peeks at a diagram.

Kidneys clean blood and balance water and salts.

They make urine to carry wastes out safely.

Two kidneys give backup if one needs extra rest.

Many people live well with one healthy kidney.

Still, two give capacity for growth, play, and illness days.

Blood flows in; cleaned blood flows back out.

Drinking water helps kidneys do their quiet job.

Foods and medicines also pass through kidney care.

Protect them: helmets, seat belts, and grown-up guidance.

You cannot see them, but they work every hour.

Twin filters, backup plan, everyday clean-up crew.

stories.title: Why Does My Stomach Growl?
stories.text:
Rumble! "Is a monster in there?" Guangguang asks.

Your stomach and intestines mix food with soft squeezes.

When empty, gas and juices slosh and make growly sounds.

Hunger hormones tell your brain it may be meal time.

Growls can also happen while digesting a big snack.

Drinking water and waiting a bit often settles the noise.

A balanced meal gives steady fuel instead of big crashes.

Everyone's tummy talks sometimes—it is not a failure.

If pain comes with growls, tell a grown-up.

Rest and calm breathing help when the rumble feels loud.

Your body is a busy kitchen, not a scary cave.

Mix, slosh, signal: tummy soundtrack science.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Chickenpox Only Once Usually?
stories.text:
Itchy dots! "Will it come back forever?" asks Guangguang.

Chickenpox is usually caused by a virus called varicella.

Your immune system learns the virus's face during illness.

Memory cells keep that lesson ready for later.

If the virus visits again, defenses often stop a full round.

That is why most people get the classic rash only once.

Vaccines teach the same lesson more gently beforehand.

Some viruses hide and can return as different itchy shingles later in life.

For kids, rest, soft clothes, and grown-up care help.

Do not scratch hard—nails can open skin to other germs.

Never share lotion guesses; ask a grown-up or doctor.

Learn once, remember long: immune school for pox.

stories.title: Why Do Babies Have Soft Spots on Their Heads?
stories.text:
A soft spot! "Is the head unfinished?" Guangguang whispers.

Babies have soft spots called fontanelles between skull bones.

Flexible gaps help the head pass through birth more safely.

They also leave room for a fast-growing baby brain.

Bones slowly meet and harden as months pass.

Gentle touch is fine; rough pressing is not a game.

Doctors check soft spots during well-baby visits.

Helmets and car seats protect growing heads on the go.

Soft spots usually close on their own with time.

If a spot looks very sunken or bulging with worry signs, tell a grown-up.

Every baby skull has a careful building plan.

Gaps for birth and growth: soft-spot science.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Saliva?
stories.text:
"Spit is gross—why make it?" Guangguang holds a napkin.

Saliva is mostly water with helpful helpers mixed in.

It moistens food so chewing and swallowing feel easier.

Enzymes in spit begin breaking some starches early.

Saliva washes teeth and helps keep the mouth less dry.

It also carries taste bits to your tongue sensors.

A dry mouth makes talking and eating harder.

Drinking water supports healthy spit production.

Brushing still matters—spit is a helper, not a toothbrush.

Spitting at people is unkind; use a sink if needed.

Your mouth makes a quiet river of useful liquid.

Moisten, start digest, wash, taste: saliva jobs.

stories.title: Why Does My Heart Beat Faster When I Run?
stories.text:
After a race, thump-thump! "Why so fast?"

Muscles need more oxygen and fuel during hard play.

Your heart pumps blood that carries those supplies.

Faster beats push more blood each minute.

Lungs work harder too, so breath may get quicker.

When you rest, the beat slows toward normal again.

A strong heart likes regular movement and sleep.

Warm up and cool down help the change feel smoother.

If chest pain or dizziness happens, stop and tell a grown-up.

Feeling your pulse on a wrist can be a calm science check.

Fast beat is your body answering the run.

Demand up, pump up, then settle: heart pacing.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Earwax?
stories.text:
"Sticky ear stuff—yuck. Why?" Guangguang peeks carefully.

Earwax is a natural cleaner and protector for the ear canal.

It traps dust and tiny bits before they go deeper.

It also helps keep the canal from getting too dry.

Old wax usually works its way out on its own.

Cotton swabs can push wax farther in—skip the dig.

A grown-up or doctor can help if hearing feels blocked.

Never pour random liquids into ears for fun.

Ears do important listening work every day.

Gentle outer cleaning of the ear flap is enough at home.

Wax is a tiny bodyguard, not dirt to dig out.

Trap, protect, migrate out: earwax jobs.

stories.title: Why Do Fingernails Grow?
stories.text:
Clip time! "Why do nails keep coming back?"

Nails grow from a root area under the skin at the base.

New cells push older cells forward into the hard plate.

The hard part is mostly keratin, a tough protein.

Nails protect fingertips and help tiny pick-up jobs.

Growth is slow and steady for most kids.

Biting nails can hurt the skin around them.

Keep nails clean and trimmed with grown-up help.

A balanced diet supports many growing body parts, including nails.

If a nail looks painful or infected, tell a grown-up.

Nails are tools and shields that quietly renew.

Root push, keratin plate, protect: nail science.

stories.title: Why Do We Get Allergies?
stories.text:
Achoo near cats! "Why does my body overreact?"

An allergy is when the immune system treats a harmless thing as a threat.

Pollen, some foods, or pet dander can be triggers for some people.

The body releases chemicals that cause itch, sneeze, or swell.

Not everyone reacts to the same triggers.

Avoiding known triggers and plans from doctors help a lot.

Allergy is different from a cold germ infection.

If breathing gets hard, get grown-up help right away.

Labels on food matter when allergies are serious.

You did nothing wrong—bodies just have different alarm settings.

Learn your triggers and keep calm helpers nearby.

False alarm, real feelings: allergy science kindly.

stories.title: Why Do We Shiver When Cold?
stories.text:
Brr! Shoulders shake. "Why shiver?" asks Guangguang.

Shivering is tiny muscle shakes that try to make heat.

Cold sensors tell your brain the body needs warming.

The brain sends a quick shake signal to many muscles.

Shaking uses energy and can raise temperature a little.

Goosebumps may join the cold response too.

A sweater, blanket, or warm drink helps more than shaking alone.

Come indoors from wind when you can.

Shivering after swimming is common until you dry and warm up.

If shivering comes with feeling very sick, tell a grown-up.

Your body has a built-in heater mode for chilly moments.

Sense cold, shake for heat, then get cozy: shiver science.

stories.title: Why Do Kids Grow So Fast Sometimes?
stories.text:
Pants suddenly short! "Did I stretch overnight?"

Kids grow in spurts when hormones and cells speed up.

Bones lengthen at growth plates near the ends.

Sleep is a big helper—repair and growth signals rise at night.

Food and protein give building blocks for new tissue.

Not every month looks the same; charts zig and zag.

Friends may grow at different times—that is normal.

Clothes and shoes get replaced as the body upgrades.

Gentle stretch and play keep growing bodies happy.

If growth worries you, a grown-up or doctor can check.

Fast seasons of growing are part of becoming you.

Spurts, sleep, fuel, plates: growth science.

stories.title: Why Do We Need Vaccines?
stories.text:
A tiny shot! "Why do we need this?" Guangguang asks kindly.

Vaccines teach your immune system before a real germ arrives.

They show a safe lesson so memory cells can practice.

Later, if the real germ comes, defenses often respond faster.

Vaccines help protect you and people around you.

Some vaccines need boosters to refresh the lesson.

A quick poke can feel scary; holding a grown-up hand helps.

Soreness or a mild fever afterward can be a training sign.

Doctors choose schedules that fit kids' ages.

Questions are welcome—ask a grown-up or nurse calmly.

Learning immunity is teamwork between science and care.

Safe lesson, strong memory, community shield: vaccine science.

stories.title: Why Does the Moon Follow Us?
stories.text:
On a car ride, the Moon seems to tag along.

Guangguang asks, "Is the Moon chasing us?"

Nearby trees zoom past the window fast.

The Moon is very, very far away.

Far things seem to move slowly beside you.

So the Moon looks like a friendly follower.

It isn't jogging after the car at all.

The Moon orbits Earth on its own path.

Distance and perspective play this cozy trick.

Many towns see the same bright Moon tonight.

Not a chase—just space looking close.

Wave hello. The Moon keeps its quiet watch.

stories.title: Why Do Stars Twinkle?
stories.text:
Stars wink above. "Blinking on purpose?"

Starlight travels a very long way to Earth.

It passes through moving layers of air.

Air bends the light a tiny bit, again and again.

To our eyes, the star seems to dance and wink.

Planets look steadier—they are closer bright disks.

Twinkle is Earth's air, not the star flipping a switch.

On a still clear night, winks can look softer.

City haze may make twinkles look busier.

Astronauts above the air see stars shine steady.

So twinkle means: light plus our restless sky.

Next clear night, watch one star gently wink.

stories.title: Why Is the Sun So Bright?
stories.text:
Sunshine pours across the room. "Ow—bright!"

The Sun is a star—our closest one.

Inside, hot gases release enormous energy.

Light and warmth race outward in every direction.

Earth catches only a tiny share of that light.

Even a tiny share is enough to light our day.

Never stare straight at the Sun—it can hurt eyes.

Use shade, hats, and sideways glances outdoors.

Sunset glow is sunlight traveling a longer path.

Night comes when our side turns away from the Sun.

Bright does not mean small—our star is huge.

Thank the Sun, then play in safe soft light.

stories.title: Why Is There No Sound in Space?
stories.text:
Clap in a pretend spacesuit. Total silence!

Sound needs something to travel through.

Usually that something is air, water, or solid stuff.

Tiny pushes pass along as a wave we hear.

Space between worlds is mostly empty of air.

With almost no air, sound waves have nowhere to go.

That is why space feels so quiet in stories.

Inside a spaceship, air lets voices work again.

On Earth, air is the everyday sound highway.

Put a bell under a jar and pump air out—quieter.

No air highway means no ordinary clap-sound.

Quiet space, noisy Earth—same science, different room.

stories.title: Why Do Rockets Need Fire?
stories.text:
A toy rocket waits. "Where's the whoosh?"

Rockets push hot gas out the bottom very fast.

Push gas one way, and the rocket goes the other way.

That push-and-go idea is how rockets climb.

The bright flame is burning fuel making fast gas.

Fire here means energy turning into a strong push.

In space there is no road—only this push matters.

Wings need air; rockets can work without wings.

Real launches are loud, carefully planned, and grown-up jobs.

Toy whooshes are pretend—never play with real fire.

Gas out the back, rocket up the front—pair of forces.

Whoosh science: push down, rise up!

stories.title: Why Do We See Only One Side of the Moon?
stories.text:
The Moon’s face looks familiar every night. "Does it spin?" asks Guangguang.

Yes—the Moon does rotate, spinning slowly like a patient top.

It takes about the same time to spin once as to go once around Earth.

That timing match is called synchronous rotation.

Because of it, we mostly see the same lunar face from Earth.

The far side still exists; it just faces away from us most of the time.

Spacecraft have photographed the far side’s different crater patterns.

There is no permanent “dark side”—both sides get sunlight over a month.

People sometimes mix up “far side” with “always dark,” but that is wrong.

Familiar Moon face is a dance of spin and orbit matched together.

Watch the Moon with a grown-up and notice the same seas and craters.

Matched spin and orbit: one-face Moon science.

stories.title: Why Are There Craters on the Moon?
stories.text:
Guangguang points at round dents. "Potholes in space?"

Long ago, rocks from space hit the Moon hard.

Those impacts left bowl-shaped craters on the surface.

The Moon has almost no air or weather to wear marks away.

So many ancient craters stay sharp for ages.

Earth gets hit too, but air, rain, and plants hide most scars.

Bigger impacts make bigger bowls; tiny ones make dimples.

Some bright rays of dust spray out from fresh-looking craters.

Astronauts and robots have studied crater edges up close.

Craters are the Moon’s history book written in stone bowls.

Look through a safe telescope with a grown-up after dark.

Impacts, no weather: crater science.

stories.title: What Is a Planet?
stories.text:
Guangguang spins a blue marble. "What is a planet?"

A planet is a big round world that orbits a star.

Earth is a planet circling our star—the Sun.

Planets are much smaller than stars and do not blaze like them.

They shine mostly by reflecting their star’s light.

Some planets are rocky; others are giant balls of gas.

Moons can orbit planets, like our Moon around Earth.

Dwarf planets are roundish worlds that share their neighborhood.

Counting planets helps us map the solar system family.

A planet is a world on a path around a shining star.

Hold a ball and walk a circle—pretend orbit with a grown-up.

Round world, star path: planet science.

stories.title: Why Does Earth Spin?
stories.text:
Day turns to night. "Who flipped the light switch?" asks Guangguang.

Earth spins like a giant top in space.

The side facing the Sun enjoys daytime.

The side turned away has nighttime darkness.

One full spin takes about twenty-four hours—our day.

Earth also travels around the Sun, making a year.

Spin and orbit together give us days, nights, and seasons helpers.

We do not feel the spin because everything moves with us.

Sunrises and sunsets are Earth’s turning in disguise.

Night is not the Sun leaving forever—just our turn away.

Watch a shadow move across a sunny yard with a grown-up.

Top-spin Earth: day-night science.

stories.title: How Many Planets Are in Our Solar System?
stories.text:
Guangguang lines up toy worlds. "Count!"

Our solar system has eight planets.

Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the inner rocky ones.

Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are the outer giants.

They all orbit the Sun on their own paths.

Dwarf planets like Pluto are smaller neighbors in the family.

Moons, asteroids, and comets fill the neighborhood too.

Learning the eight names is a fun space song for kids.

Telescopes and spacecraft help us check each world.

Eight planets share one star’s warm neighborhood.

Line up fruit or toys with a grown-up and name each one.

Eight worlds, one Sun: solar-system count science.

stories.title: What Is a Comet?
stories.text:
A fuzzy visitor streaks. "Comet?" asks Guangguang.

A comet is a dirty snowball of ice, dust, and rock.

Far from the Sun it stays cold and quiet.

Near the Sun, ice turns to gas and dust lifts off.

That material streams into a glowing tail.

The tail always points away from the Sun’s push and light.

Some comets return on long oval paths after many years.

People once thought comets were omens; now we know they are icy travelers.

Never stare at the Sun while hunting comets—use safe tools with help.

A comet is a thawing snowball on a long trip through space.

Draw a snowball with a tail for fun after the story.

Ice, dust, glowing tail: comet science.

stories.title: What Is an Asteroid?
stories.text:
Rocky dots between planets. "Asteroids?" asks Guangguang.

Asteroids are rocky leftover pieces from the solar system’s youth.

Most live in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Some are as small as cars; others are much bigger.

They do not have glowing comet tails of ice and dust.

Spacecraft have visited asteroids to take close pictures.

Scientists study them to learn how planets began.

A few asteroids cross near Earth—we track them carefully.

Movies make giant scary rocks; real tracking keeps us informed.

Asteroids are leftover building blocks of rocky worlds.

Sort pebbles by size for a gentle “belt” game with a grown-up.

Rocky leftovers: asteroid science.

stories.title: Why Is Mars Red?
stories.text:
A rusty marble in the sky. "Why red?" asks Guangguang.

Mars soil has lots of iron oxide—like rust on Earth.

Dust in the air can tint the whole planet reddish.

It is colder and drier than Earth overall.

Polar ice caps shine at the top and bottom.

Giant volcanoes and deep canyons mark its surface.

Rovers roll around taking photos and testing rocks.

People nicknamed it the Red Planet for the rusty look.

Red does not mean hot lava everywhere—much of Mars is chilly.

Rust-colored dust is the fashion of this neighboring world.

Compare orange chalk dust to gray pebbles with a grown-up.

Iron rust dust: Mars-red science.

stories.title: What Is the Milky Way?
stories.text:
A milky band crosses the dark sky. "Our galaxy?" asks Guangguang.

The Milky Way is the huge star city we live inside.

It holds billions of stars plus gas and dust.

Many of those stars form a flat spiral shape.

From Earth we often see it edge-on as a pale river of light.

Other galaxies shine far beyond our own star city.

Telescopes are the ships that help us explore farther.

Dark skies away from city glow show the band best.

We are not outside looking in—we are riding inside it.

The Milky Way is home, not a splash of spilled milk.

Ask a grown-up for a dark-sky night when you can.

Star city spiral: Milky Way science.

stories.title: Why Do Astronauts Float in Space?
stories.text:
Guangguang pretends to float. "Zero gravity?"

In orbit, astronauts and their ship fall around Earth together.

Everything falls at about the same rate.

Because of that, people feel weightless inside the craft.

It is like continuous freefall without hitting the ground.

Gravity did not vanish—Earth still pulls.

The fast sideways speed keeps the fall curved into orbit.

Floating hair and water blobs are famous orbit sights.

Exercise helps astronauts keep muscles strong up there.

Weightless feeling is freefall teamwork, not magic off-switch.

Jump gently on a trampoline with a grown-up and notice floaty moments.

Fall together, feel float: orbit science.

stories.title: What Is a Black Hole?
stories.text:
A dark circle on a diagram. "Scary?" asks Guangguang gently.

A black hole is a place where gravity is extremely strong.

Inside a boundary called the event horizon, light cannot escape.

Some form when very massive stars collapse at the end of life.

They are not hungry monsters roaming to eat everything nearby.

Far away, their pull is just gravity—like any massive object.

Scientists study them with math, telescopes, and careful pictures.

A famous image showed a glowing ring around one shadow.

Curiosity is fine; nightmares are not required.

Black holes are extreme gravity neighborhoods in space.

Look at soft diagrams with a grown-up, not spooky movies only.

Strong gravity, no escape light: black-hole science kindly.

stories.title: Why Is Venus So Hot?
stories.text:
A bright morning “star.” "Hotter than Mercury?" asks Guangguang.

Venus wears a thick blanket of carbon-dioxide air.

That atmosphere traps heat like a runaway greenhouse.

Surface temperatures climb oven-hot.

Mercury is closer to the Sun, yet Venus can be hotter.

The thick air, not just distance, drives the heat story.

Clouds hide the surface from ordinary eyesight.

Probes and telescopes study Venus from safer distances.

Earth’s air is different—our greenhouse is milder with care.

Venus heat is a thick-air trap more than a near-Sun prize.

Compare a jacket greenhouse to a thin T-shirt with a grown-up.

Thick air trap: Venus-hot science.

stories.title: What Are Saturn’s Rings Made Of?
stories.text:
Sparkly rings around Saturn. "Ice?" asks Guangguang.

Saturn’s rings are countless chunks of ice and rock.

Some pieces are tiny; some are boulder-sized.

They orbit in thin sheets like glittering traffic lanes.

Moonlets and gravity sculpt gaps and waves in the rings.

From far away the rings look solid and smooth.

Up close they are a busy icy rubble highway.

Spacecraft have flown near to photograph the details.

Other giant planets have rings too, often fainter.

Rings are icy rubble highways, not magic hoops.

Spin a hula hoop gently and imagine many tiny moons inside.

Ice, rock, orbit sheets: ring science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Seasons?
stories.text:
Summer sweat, winter coats. "Why seasons?" asks Guangguang.

Earth’s axis is tilted as we travel around the Sun.

For part of the year one hemisphere leans toward sunlight.

That leaning side gets warmer months.

The other hemisphere leans away and gets cooler months.

Distance to the Sun changes a little, but tilt drives seasons.

Near the equator, season changes can feel milder.

Near the poles, summer light and winter dark get extreme.

Calendars and festivals often celebrate these shifts.

Seasons are a tilt dance, not Earth hopping closer then farther only.

Shine a flashlight on a tilted globe with a grown-up.

Tilted axis orbit: season science.

stories.title: What Is the International Space Station?
stories.text:
A metal butterfly in orbit. "ISS?" asks Guangguang.

The International Space Station is a flying science lab.

Astronauts from many countries live and work there.

It circles Earth about once every ninety minutes.

They study science in microgravity and test life in space.

Cargo ships bring food, tools, and experiments.

Solar panels gather sunlight to power the station.

Crews exercise so bones and muscles stay healthier.

Sometimes you can spot it as a bright moving dot at night.

The ISS is a shared home lab above the clouds.

Track a pass time online with a grown-up and wave hello.

Orbit lab teamwork: ISS science.

stories.title: Why Do Meteors Streak?
stories.text:
A quick scratch of light. "Shooting star?" asks Guangguang.

A meteor is a space rock racing through Earth’s air.

Friction heats it until it glows as a streak.

Most meteors are tiny and burn up high above.

If a piece survives and lands, it is called a meteorite.

Meteor showers happen when Earth crosses dusty trails.

Wishes are optional—the physics happens either way.

Never confuse meteors with airplanes’ steady lights.

Safe watching means eyes on the sky, feet on the ground.

Meteor streaks are air-friction fireworks from tiny rocks.

Lie on a blanket with a grown-up on a clear night.

Glow, streak, maybe land: meteor science.

stories.title: What Is a Light-Year?
stories.text:
Guangguang draws a ruler across stars. "Light-year?"

A light-year measures distance, not birthday time.

It is how far light travels in one whole year.

That stretch is about 9.5 trillion kilometers.

Stars are so far that ordinary miles feel tiny and silly.

Saying “four light-years away” packs a huge trip into short words.

Light is the fastest messenger we know in empty space.

When you see a star, its light may be years old already.

Telescopes collect that old light like bottles of travel stories.

Light-years turn huge space into numbers we can say out loud.

Imagine a beam racing while Earth orbits once—then smile at the size.

Distance stick of light: light-year science.

stories.title: Why Does the Sun Rise in the East?
stories.text:
Morning gold. "Always east?" asks Guangguang.

Earth spins from west toward east.

From the ground, the Sun seems to climb in the east.

Later it seems to set toward the west.

The Sun is not racing around us each day—we are turning.

That spin paints sunrise and sunset on the sky.

Poles and seasons can tweak the Sun’s path a bit.

Compasses still help hikers keep directions straight.

Noon is when the Sun is highest for your place.

Sunrise direction is Earth’s spin written in light.

Watch a morning with a grown-up and point east together.

West-to-east spin: sunrise science.

stories.title: What Are Constellations?
stories.text:
Dot-to-dot bears and hunters. "Real groups?" asks Guangguang.

Constellations are patterns people imagined in the stars.

We connect dots as seen from Earth into sky pictures.

Stars in one pattern may not be neighbors in real space.

They can just line up from our viewpoint.

Different cultures drew different sky stories.

Astronomers still use the names as handy sky maps.

Learning a few patterns helps you find your way at night.

Apps and grown-ups can point out the bright landmarks.

Constellations are storytelling overlays on distant suns.

Trace one simple shape on paper after looking up together.

Sky stories on real stars: constellation science.

stories.title: Why Do Shadows Follow Us?
stories.text:
Guangguang spins. The shadow spins too!

A shadow appears when something blocks light.

Light hits you; a dark shape falls behind.

Move left—the blocked spot moves left.

That's why the shadow seems to follow.

Move the lamp, and shadows stretch or shrink.

At noon the Sun is high; shadows stay short.

Later, long shadows walk across the ground.

Soft light makes fuzzy edges; hard light looks sharp.

Shadows are light's quiet footprints.

No feet of their own—just blocked brightness.

Dance once. Your shadow dances with you.

stories.title: Why Does Ice Melt?
stories.text:
An ice cube drips. "Disappearing act!"

Ice is water frozen into a solid shape.

Heat gives tiny bits of water more energy.

They slip free of the stiff ice pattern.

Then ice becomes liquid water you can pour.

Warm air can melt a cube on the table.

Warm hands melt ice even faster.

Sunlight adds heat on a bright day too.

Melting is not vanishing into nothing.

It is water changing form—solid to liquid.

Freeze it again and water can become ice.

Same water, different costume—cool science!

stories.title: Why Do Soap Bubbles Float?
stories.text:
A bubble drifts up, then pops!

A bubble is a thin soap-water skin.

Inside the skin is a pocket of air.

Soap makes that skin stretchy and strong.

Warm air inside can help it lift a bit.

Gentle breezes can carry bubbles along.

Gravity still pulls, so they do not fly forever.

As the skin dries, it gets thinner.

When it thins too much—pop!

Bubbles teach thin films and air together.

Sparkle colors dance on the soap skin.

Blow softly, watch, then smile at the pop.

stories.title: Why Do Balloons Float Up?
stories.text:
A helium balloon tugs the string skyward.

Helium is lighter than the air around us.

A balloon full of helium weighs less.

Less than the same-sized blob of regular air.

Denser air pushes up, so the balloon rises.

It is a bit like wood floating on water—but in air.

Regular breath balloons usually fall down.

Your breath is not lighter than outside air.

Hold strings gently when you walk outside.

Let balloons go only where it is safe.

And only where grown-ups say it is allowed.

Light gas, gentle hands, happy sky tug!

stories.title: Why Do Some Things Float?
stories.text:
A leaf rides a puddle; a pebble sinks.

Floating depends on density—how packed stuff is.

Shape matters too, not only weight.

If something pushes aside heavy water, it can float.

The water it moves can weigh more than the object.

Boats use hollow shapes to displace lots of water.

That is why a big empty boat can float.

Heavy metal can float as a boat shape.

But the same metal as a tight ball may sink.

Shape and density work as a team.

Try a leaf, a pebble, and a toy boat.

Watch who rides—and who takes a dive!

stories.title: Why Can We See Ourselves in Mirrors?
stories.text:
Guangguang waves; the glass waves back. "How?"

A mirror’s smooth surface reflects light in an orderly way.

Light from your face bounces to your eyes as a clear image.

Ordinary walls scatter light messily in many directions.

Mirrors bounce light neatly like a tidy bounce house for photons.

Left and right look swapped in the usual bathroom-mirror way.

That swap is geometry with shine, not magic twin tricks.

Curved mirrors can stretch or shrink what you see.

Telescopes and cars use mirrors to send light where needed.

Wipe gently—scratches scatter the neat bounce.

Seeing yourself is light making a round trip.

Orderly bounce: mirror science.

stories.title: What Makes a Plane Fly?
stories.text:
A plane lifts off. "How does it stay up?" asks Guangguang.

Airplane wings are shaped to help create lift—an upward push.

Engines move the plane forward so air flows fast over the wings.

Fast airflow and wing shape work together for flight.

Pilots and flaps adjust the wing for takeoff and landing.

Birds flap and change shape; planes use engines and fixed wings.

Same sky, different toolkits for staying aloft.

Air traffic rules keep many planes sharing the sky safely.

Watch takeoffs from a safe airport overlook with a grown-up.

Lift is not magic—it is moving air doing a job.

Forward speed plus wing shape equals a flying machine.

Airflow and lift: plane science.

stories.title: How Does a Simple Wheel Help?
stories.text:
Guangguang rolls a toy car. "So smooth!"

Wheels turn hard sliding into easier rolling motion.

Rolling usually takes less effort than dragging a box.

Axles hold wheels so carts and bikes can carry loads.

Round shapes keep contact small and motion steady.

Scooters, suitcases, and skateboards all borrow the idea.

Without wheels, many heavy jobs would scrap and scrape.

Oil and air in tires keep real wheels happier.

A stuck pebble can turn a smooth roll into a bump—pick it safely.

From ancient carts to cars, the round idea still moves the world.

Try rolling versus dragging a book with a grown-up’s okay.

Rolling beats dragging: wheel science.

stories.title: Why Do Boats Float?
stories.text:
A toy boat sits high. "Heavy boats float—how?" asks Guangguang.

Water pushes up on anything that pushes water aside.

That upward push can equal the boat’s weight.

A boat’s hollow shape spreads weight over enough water.

A solid steel cube may sink; a steel hull shaped like a bowl can float.

Holes that flood the hull spoil the floating trick.

Life jackets help people stay up by adding floaty volume.

Density and shape team up more than “being light” alone.

Calm pools are safer places to test toy boats with a grown-up.

Floating is a push-up contest between object and water.

Respect deep water—float science still needs life rules.

Shape, push, float: boat science.

stories.title: Why Do Rubber Bands Snap Back?
stories.text:
Twang! "Why does it bounce back?" asks Guangguang.

Rubber has long tangled molecules like stretchy noodles.

Pulling straightens them and stores energy in the stretch.

Let go and the molecules tug toward their relaxed shape.

That springiness returns the band—until it finally breaks.
