Heat and old age can make rubber crackly and weak.

Never aim rubber bands at faces or animals.

Physics is cool; safety is cooler.

Other elastic things—hair ties, some toys—use similar stretch ideas.

Snap-back is molecular springs doing tiny yoga.

Stretch gently for science demos with a grown-up watching.

Store, return, rest: rubber-band science.

stories.title: Why Do Bike Gears Help Hills?
stories.text:
Pedal grind on a hill. "What do gears do?" asks Guangguang.

Gears trade turning force and speed like a mechanical translator.

A low gear makes pedaling easier uphill but you go slower.

A high gear covers ground faster on flats with more effort per turn.

The chain carries spin from pedals to the rear wheel.

Clicking into the right gear matches your legs to the hill.

Oil and clean care keep gear rides smooth.

Walking the bike is okay if the hill still feels too hard.

Helmets matter more than any fancy gear trick.

Gears do not remove work—they reshape how hard each pedal feels.

Practice shifting on a quiet path with a grown-up.

Force and speed trade: bike-gear science.

stories.title: Why Do Speakers Make Sound?
stories.text:
Music shakes the air. "How?" asks Guangguang.

A speaker cone moves back and forth very quickly.

That motion pushes air into waves your ears hear as sound.

Electricity and magnets drive the cone following the music signal.

Bigger waves can mean louder sounds; smaller waves can mean softer ones.

Different speeds of shaking help make high and low notes.

Phones, TVs, and concert stacks all use versions of this idea.

Too-loud volume can hurt ears—ask a grown-up to keep it gentle.

Covering a speaker muffles the air waves and softens the song.

Sound is shaking air that reaches your eardrums.

Dance a little when the cone makes the room hum kindly.

Cone, magnet, air waves: speaker science.

stories.title: Why Do Fridges Stay Cold Inside?
stories.text:
Cold lettuce, warm kitchen. "How?" asks Guangguang.

A fridge does not make a bag of coldness—it moves heat out.

A special fluid cycles through pipes, picking up indoor heat.

The warm heat is dumped to coils on the back or bottom.

Inside stays cooler while the kitchen gets a little of that heat.

The door seal keeps warm room air from rushing back in.

Opening the door a long time invites warmth to sneak inside.

Dusty coils work harder—grown-ups sometimes wipe them carefully.

Freezers are colder cousins using a similar heat-moving trick.

Food stays fresher when heat is pumped away on purpose.

Feel the warm coils with a grown-up’s okay—science you can touch.

Move heat out: fridge science.

stories.title: Why Do Straws Make Drinking Easier?
stories.text:
Slurp! "Is it a vacuum magic?" asks Guangguang.

When you suck, you lower air pressure inside the straw.

Higher outside air pressure pushes the drink up toward your mouth.

You are not lifting the juice with pure willpower alone.

Air is a quiet helper shoving the liquid up the tube.

Pinch the straw and the push path gets blocked.

Very tall straws fight gravity more—sips get harder.

Reusable straws work the same physics with less trash.

Don’t share straws when someone is sick—germs hitch rides.

Pressure difference is the real straw superpower.

Try a short sip experiment with a grown-up watching.

Lower inside, push up: straw science.

stories.title: Why Do Flashlights Need Batteries?
stories.text:
Click—a beam! "Why batteries?" asks Guangguang.

Batteries store chemical energy ready to become electricity.

That current can heat a filament or power bright LEDs.

Without a power source, the bulb stays dark.

The switch completes the circuit so electricity can flow.

Dead batteries mean the chemical store is used up.

Rechargeable packs can refill; others get recycled with help.

Never put batteries in mouths—they are not snacks.

A flashlight is a tiny portable power-and-light team.

Camping and power outages make that team feel heroic.

Check the + and − ends so the current knows its path.

Chemical store to light: flashlight science.

stories.title: Why Do Bridges Have Triangles?
stories.text:
Steel triangles rise. "Why that shape?" asks Guangguang.

Triangles are strong and stable under pushes and pulls.

Push a triangle’s corner and the sides share the force.

A floppy square can squash into a slant more easily.

Bridge builders lace triangles into trusses for strength.

Cars and trains send weight that triangles help carry.

Wood craft sticks can make tiny triangle bridges for demos.

Circles and arches are strong too—in different jobs.

Look for triangles next time you cross with a grown-up.

Shape is a silent tool as important as the steel itself.

Engineers choose geometry so people and cargo stay safe.

Stable three sides: bridge-triangle science.

stories.title: Why Do Matches Light When Scratched?
stories.text:
Scratch—flame. Grown-up only. "How?" whispers Guangguang.

Friction heat starts a chemical reaction in the match head.

Special chemicals catch fire more easily than plain wood.

Safety matches need the special strip on the box to light.

Strike-anywhere matches are still not toys for kids.

Fire needs fuel, heat, and air—scratch supplies the heat spark.

Never play with matches; ask a grown-up for any demo.

Blow gently or use water to put out practice flames safely.

Lighters and stoves follow related heat-and-fuel ideas.

Respect fire: it cooks food and also can hurt.

Science explains the scratch; rules keep fingers safe.

Friction, chemistry, care: match science.

stories.title: Why Do Sunglasses Help?
stories.text:
Bright glare. Dark lenses. "Just fashion?" asks Guangguang.

Good sunglasses cut harsh light that makes eyes squint.

Many also block invisible ultraviolet rays that stress eyes over time.

Polarized lenses tame bounce glare from water and roads.

Fashion frames are fun; protection labels matter more.

Hats and shade help too on blazing days.

Never stare at the Sun even with glasses—look away.

Kids’ eyes deserve gentle light as much as grown-ups’ do.

Store glasses in a case so scratches don’t scatter light.

Comfortable seeing helps you play longer outdoors.

Ask a grown-up for UV-protecting pair when shopping.

Cut glare, block UV: sunglass science.

stories.title: Why Do Clocks Tick?
stories.text:
Tick-tock. "Why the sound?" asks Guangguang.

Many clocks move gears in tiny careful steps.

Escapement parts catch and release, making the tick.

Each tick marks a small slice of time marching forward.

Quartz clocks use a vibrating crystal for steady timing.

Their tick can be a speaker click copying that rhythm.

Silent digital clocks hide the steps behind a screen.

Pendulum clocks swing a weight to keep the pace.

Timekeepers help schools, trains, and bedtimes stay fair.

Listen to a wind-up clock with a grown-up—gentle science music.

The sound is machinery counting, not a tiny insect.

Catch, release, count: clock-tick science.

stories.title: Why Do Microwaves Heat Food Fast?
stories.text:
Beep. Steam rises. "How so quick?" asks Guangguang.

Microwave ovens make special waves inside a metal box.

Those waves jostle water molecules in the food.

Jostling molecules make heat from the inside, not only the outside.

A regular oven mostly warms from the outside in, which can take longer.

Metal and some containers are unsafe—follow the manual with a grown-up.

Stirring helps heat spread more evenly through the food.

Hot spots can burn tongues, so wait and test carefully.

Covers can reduce splatters while waves still reach the meal.

Microwaves are water-molecule dance floors in a careful metal box.

Never run empty tricks—ask a grown-up before any experiment.

Waves jostle water: microwave science.

stories.title: Why Do Parachutes Slow Falls?
stories.text:
A silk umbrella blooms. "Why safer?" asks Guangguang.

A parachute catches a lot of air as it opens.

That big catch makes a drag force pushing upward against the fall.

More area means more air resistance, so the descent slows.

Free fall without a chute is much faster and not a game.

Skydiving needs serious training—kids watch, not jump.

Toy parachutes can show the idea safely indoors with a grown-up.

Lines and canopy shape help the chute stay steady.

Emergency chutes on some planes are carefully packed tools.

Parachutes buy time by hugging a lot of air.

Respect height rules on playgrounds and balconies always.

Catch air, slow down: parachute science.

stories.title: Why Do Locks Need Keys?
stories.text:
Click. The door opens. "How?" asks Guangguang.

A key’s jagged edge lifts tiny pins inside the lock.

When pins reach the matching height, the cylinder can turn.

Wrong keys leave pins blocking so the lock stays shut.

It is a tiny three-dimensional puzzle made of metal.

Digital locks use codes or cards instead of teeth.

Keep spare keys in a safe place with a grown-up’s plan.

Never hide house keys under the mat for strangers to find.

Oil and gentle care keep old locks from sticking.

Keys are portable answers to a pin puzzle in metal.

Ask before borrowing keys—they open more than toys.

Pins, teeth, turn: lock-and-key science.

stories.title: Why Do Fans Cool Us If They Don’t Make Cold Air?
stories.text:
Whirr. "The air isn’t icy—why cooler?" asks Guangguang.

Fans move air across your skin in a steady breeze.

Moving air helps sweat evaporate faster.

When sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from your body.

The room air temperature may stay about the same.

You feel cooler because heat leaves your skin quicker.

In a sealed empty room with no people, a fan mostly just stirs air.

Open windows can help move humid air out on sticky days.

Keep fingers away from spinning blades—covers matter.

Fan “cool” is evaporating-sweat express, not fridge wind.

Sip water too; fans help comfort, not magic freeze.

Breeze, evaporate, cool: fan science.

stories.title: Why Do Velcro Stick and Peel?
stories.text:
Rrrrip! "How does it stick and peel?" asks Guangguang.

Velcro pairs tiny hooks with tiny loops.

Pressing lets hooks catch the loops and hold on.

Peeling unhooks them with that famous ripping sound.

The idea was inspired by burrs stuck on clothes after a walk.

Nature’s hitchhikers taught a useful fastening trick.

Dirt fills loops and weakens the grip over time.

A brush or gentle clean helps fuzzy sides work again.

Shoes, bags, and jackets often use hook-and-loop strips.

Velcro is miniature grappling hooks taught by burrs.

Press firm, peel slow—and laugh at the rrrrip.

Hooks meet loops: Velcro science.

stories.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
stories.text:
Guangguang looks up. Blue forever!

Sunlight holds many colors mixed together.

Air molecules scatter blue light the most.

Red light scatters less on its way.

Looking away from the Sun, more blue reaches our eyes.

That is why daytime sky looks blue.

Near the Sun, light can look brighter white-gold.

Space looks black—there is almost no air there.

Without air, light does not scatter the same way.

Earth's air paints our blue ceiling.

Same sunlight, special sky paint.

Next sunny day, thank the tiny air helpers.

stories.title: Why Is the Sunset Red?
stories.text:
Evening turns peach and red.

At sunset, sunlight travels through more air.

Blue light scatters out of the long path.

Reds and oranges travel farther to your eyes.

Dust and clouds can deepen the colors.

Same Sun—longer path, warmer colors.

Morning sunrise can wear similar warm coats.

City haze may make reds look extra deep.

Clean air still makes soft peach evenings.

Sunsets are physics wearing a pretty coat.

Watch safely—never stare hard at the Sun.

Wave goodnight to the warm sky.

stories.title: Why Does It Rain?
stories.text:
Drops tap the window. Tap tap!

Warm air lifts invisible water vapor up.

High up, the air cools.

Tiny droplets gather into clouds.

Droplets grow heavier and heavier.

Gravity pulls them down as rain.

Rain waters plants and thirsty soil.

Rain helps fill rivers and lakes.

Too much rain can make puddle floods.

Too little rain makes dry, thirsty days.

Weather is Earth's water on the move.

Listen—rain is the sky sharing a drink.

stories.title: Why Does Thunder Follow Lightning?
stories.text:
Flash first… then comes the boom.

Lightning is a giant spark in the sky.

The spark heats air incredibly fast.

Hot air expands in a sudden shock.

That shock is the sound we call thunder.

Light races much faster than sound.

So we see the flash before we hear the rumble.

Counting seconds after a flash can hint distance.

But the safe rule is simpler.

If you hear thunder, head indoors.

Go with a grown-up. Stay cozy and dry.

Storm science and storm safety stay together.

stories.title: Why Does It Snow?
stories.text:
Soft flakes fall. Quiet white!

When clouds are cold enough, water can freeze.

Ice crystals begin to grow.

Crystals stick together into flakes.

Flakes drift down if the air stays cold.

If air is too warm, flakes may melt to rain.

Every flake grows with a pattern.

No two flake journeys are identical.

Snow is winter's quiet rain of crystals.

Snow can blanket soil and sleep seeds.

Boots, hats, and gentle play keep toes warm.

Catch one flake—then smile at winter science.

stories.title: Why Do Rainbows Appear?
stories.text:
After a shower, colors arc across the sky.

Guangguang points. "Where did that bow come from?"

Sunlight slips into tiny raindrops.

Inside each drop, light bends and reflects.

Different colors bend by different amounts.

Red, orange, yellow—then green to violet.

You need sun behind you and drops ahead.

The bow isn't a road you can walk on.

It's light's geometry painted in water.

Move a little; the rainbow seems to move too.

Same sunshine, same drops—new place to stand.

After rain, look opposite the Sun and smile.

stories.title: Why Does the Wind Blow?
stories.text:
Leaves dance. "Who pushes the air?" asks Guangguang.

Sun warms some places more than others.

Warm air rises and cooler air slides in to fill the space.

That moving air is wind we feel on our faces.

Big weather patterns make breezes and stronger gusts.

Mountains and oceans can steer how wind flows.

A gentle breeze helps fly a kite on a safe open day.

Strong storms need grown-up plans—stay inside when told.

Windmills can turn moving air into useful power.

Feel wind safely; never chase storms for fun.

Air is invisible, but wind shows it is busy.

Warm rise, cool slide, moving air: wind science.

stories.title: Why Do Clouds Look Fluffy?
stories.text:
Cotton candy sky! "Are clouds pillows?"

Clouds are tiny water drops or ice bits floating together.

From far away, the crowd of drops looks soft and fluffy.

Up close they are wet mist, not stuffed toys.

Different cloud shapes form in different air layers.

Fluffy cumulus often grow on fair sunny days.

Gray sheets can mean steady rain is coming.

Wind stretches clouds into streaks across the blue.

Planes fly through clouds—pilots train for that carefully.

Watch clouds from the ground; don't climb toward storms.

Fluffy looks are a crowd of tiny floaters.

Drops, distance, soft look: cloud science.

stories.title: Why Do We See Lightning Before Thunder?
stories.text:
Flash! Then boom. "Why the wait?"

Lightning is a giant spark of electricity in the sky.

Light races to your eyes almost instantly.

Thunder is the sound of air jumping from the heat.

Sound travels much slower than light through air.

So the flash arrives first; the rumble follows.

Counting seconds between flash and boom estimates distance.

Stay safe indoors during thunderstorms.

Never stand under a lone tall tree in a storm.

Lightning is powerful—admire from a safe place.

Light wins the race; sound comes second.

Flash first, boom later: storm timing science.

stories.title: What Is Fog?
stories.text:
White morning air! "Is fog a cloud hug?"

Fog is a cloud that forms near the ground.

Tiny water drops hang in cool moist air.

When air cools enough, water vapor becomes visible droplets.

Fog makes lights look soft and fuzzy.

Drivers go slow because seeing far is harder.

Sea coasts and valleys often get foggy mornings.

Sun warmth can lift and clear the fog later.

Walking in fog feels magical but stay with a grown-up.

Fog is weather you can almost touch.

Tiny floaters near the ground make the white veil.

Ground cloud, tiny drops, soft world: fog science.

stories.title: Why Do Deserts Get Cold at Night?
stories.text:
Hot sand by day, chilly night! "Why the flip?"

Deserts often have dry air with little moisture.

Dry air does not hold heat as well after sunset.

With few clouds, heat escapes to the open sky.

Day sun bakes the ground; night lets warmth leave.

Temperature can drop a lot between noon and midnight.

Layered clothes help travelers handle the swing.

Animals may rest in shade by day and move at dusk.

Water and planning matter in desert trips with grown-ups.

Stars shine bright when desert nights turn clear and crisp.

Hot and cold can share the same sandy place.

Dry air, open sky, heat escape: desert night science.

stories.title: Why Do Hurricanes Spin?
stories.text:
A spinning storm on the map! "Why the swirl?"

Hurricanes are huge storms that form over warm ocean water.

Rising moist air fuels tall storm clouds.

Earth's spin helps steer the storm into a rotating swirl.

That effect is called the Coriolis effect in science class.

Winds circle around a calmer center called the eye.

Hurricane watches mean families prepare early.

Follow grown-up and weather service safety plans.

Never go outside to watch dangerous winds.

Warm water, rising air, Earth spin: swirl recipe.

Respect big storms; learn from safe screens and books.

Spin science keeps us curious and careful.

stories.title: What Is Hail?
stories.text:
Ice pellets bounce! "Is hail frozen rain?"

Hail forms in strong thunderstorms with tall cold clouds.

Tiny ice bits get coated with water that freezes again.

Updrafts toss the growing ice balls up and down.

When they grow heavy, they fall as hailstones.

Hail can be pea-sized or sometimes larger.

Car roofs and gardens may need cover during hail.

Stay indoors until the bouncing ice stops.

Hail is not the same as soft winter snowflakes.

Thunderstorm engines can make summer ice.

Up, coat, fall: hail factory science.

Respect hail; watch from a safe window.

stories.title: Why Is the Sky Dark at Night?
stories.text:
Day blue, night black. "Where did the light go?"

At night our side of Earth turns away from the Sun.

Without daytime sunlight, the sky looks dark.

Stars were there all along—sunlight hides them by day.

City lights can brighten the night and hide faint stars.

The Moon reflects sunlight and can glow softly.

Night helps many animals hunt or rest on their schedules.

Sleepy humans use night for rest and dreams.

Look at stars with a grown-up in a safe open place.

Darkness is Earth's night-side view of space.

Turn away from Sun, stars show: night sky science.

Blue day, dark night—one spinning planet.

stories.title: Why Do Puddles Disappear?
stories.text:
Morning puddle, noon dry. "Where did it go?" asks Guangguang.

Sun and warm air give water energy to turn into invisible vapor.

That jump from liquid to vapor is called evaporation.

Wind brushes the surface and whisks vapor away faster.

The puddle did not fall into another dimension—it joined the air.

Bigger puddles hold more water, so they last longer.

Shade and cool air slow the drying, so some spots stay wet.

Tiny leftover rings of dirt show where the edge used to be.

The same water may later make a cloud, then rain again.

So disappearing puddles are slow-motion steam without a teapot whistle.

Watch one puddle with a grown-up after rain—science in the sidewalk.

Sun, air, wind: puddle vanishing science.

stories.title: What Is Humidity?
stories.text:
Sticky air hugs everyone. "What is humidity?" asks Guangguang.

Humidity measures how much water vapor the air is holding.

High humidity means lots of invisible water already in the air.

Then sweat evaporates slowly, so skin feels muggy and clingy.

Low humidity means drier air that can chap lips and static hair.

Weather apps often show a humidity percent for the day.

A fan helps by moving moist still air across your skin.

Bathrooms fog up fast because warm water adds vapor indoors.

Plants and wet clothes also release water into room air.

Feeling sticky is not a failure—it is vapor chemistry on you.

Dress light, sip water, and rest in shade when air is heavy.

Invisible water load: humidity science.

stories.title: Why Do Weather Maps Use Colors?
stories.text:
A blob of green and red. "What does that mean?" asks Guangguang.

Weather maps paint data so your eyes grasp patterns fast.

Colors can show rain strength, temperature bands, or radar echoes.

On many rain maps, green is lighter rain and yellow or red means heavier.

Every map has a key—read it like a legend for the colors.

Forecasts guess tomorrow; your window confirms today.

Dress for the color story: coat for cold blues, rain gear for wet greens.

Satellites and radars feed the colorful pictures scientists draw.

Colors are shortcuts, not magic paint that makes weather.

Ask a grown-up to decode a map before a big trip.

Busy numbers become a picture kids can scan in seconds.

Color shortcuts for sky data: map science.

stories.title: Why Does Dew Form on Grass?
stories.text:
Morning sparkles on grass. "Did it rain overnight?" asks Guangguang.

Clear nights let the ground cool after the sun goes away.

Air near the blades can cool until it cannot hold all its vapor.

Extra vapor becomes tiny droplets—dew—on leaves and grass.

Dew is condensation jewelry, not always rain from clouds.

Shoes get wet on purpose when you walk the sparkling lawn.

As the day warms, dew evaporates back into the air.

Frost is related but frozen—ice crystals instead of liquid beads.

Garden spiders’ webs look jeweled when dew clings to silk.

Farmers once watched dew as a clue about cool clear nights.

Step gently and notice how cold grass can make water appear.

Cool ground, clingy vapor: dew science.

stories.title: What Causes a Drought?
stories.text:
Cracked earth under a bright sky. "Why so little rain?" asks Guangguang.

A drought is a long stretch with less water than plants and people need.

Stubborn weather patterns can park dry air over a region for weeks.

Rivers, soil, and reservoirs slowly shrink when rain stays away.

People’s water use also matters when supplies run thin.

Conservation—short showers, fixing leaks—helps communities cope.

Lawns can wait; drinking water and farms matter more.

Follow local water rules posted by grown-ups and cities.

Drought is a water budget gone thin for too long.

Scientists watch rainfall totals and soil moisture for warnings.

Hope returns when storms finally refill the land’s savings.

Thin water budget: drought science kindly.

stories.title: Why Do Weather Balloons Go Up?
stories.text:
A giant balloon lifts a little box. "Why send it up?" asks Guangguang.

Weather balloons carry sensors through layers of sky.

As they rise, gadgets measure temperature, humidity, and pressure.

Radios send those numbers down so forecasts can improve.

High up the balloon stretches and finally bursts safely by design.

A parachute helps the instrument package float back down.

They are science messengers, not party balloons for cake.

Twice a day in many places, teams launch them for global data.

Planes and models use that sky notebook to steer safer flights.

Watch a launch with a grown-up if a weather station invites kids.

Each flight is a flying notebook for the atmosphere’s layers.

Rise, measure, radio home: balloon science.

stories.title: Why Is Snow Quiet?
stories.text:
Soft footsteps hush the street. "Why so quiet?" asks Guangguang.

Fresh snow is packed with tiny air pockets between flakes.

Those pockets soak up sound waves like gentle acoustic foam.

City noise sounds muffled after a thick new blizzard.

When snow melts or packs hard, the hush fades away.

Ice alone is louder under boots than fluffy powder.

Enjoy the quiet walk—then shovel with a grown-up’s plan.

Animals leave soft tracks that barely crackle in deep powder.

Wind can still whistle above, even when ground snow muffles.

Quiet snow is physics you can feel in your ears.

Bundle up, listen closely, and thank the fluffy blanket.

Air pockets hush the world: snow quiet science.

stories.title: What Is the Jet Stream?
stories.text:
A fast ribbon on the forecast map. "Jet stream?" asks Guangguang.

Jet streams are swift rivers of wind high up in the sky.

They steer weather systems like invisible sky freeways.

Planes sometimes ride a jet stream to save time on long trips.

The ribbon wiggles and shifts as seasons change.

Cold and warm air meeting helps build these fast currents.

They are not airplane-only highways—storms ride them too.

Forecasters watch the jet stream to guess where rain may go.

You cannot see it from the ground, but maps sketch its path.

High and fast, it still follows physics, not magic rails.

Next flight delay or early arrival may thank that wind river.

Sky freeway for storms and jets: jet-stream science.

stories.title: Why Do Windows Fog on Cold Days?
stories.text:
Steamy glass on a cold day. "Fog inside?" asks Guangguang.

Warm moist indoor air drifts toward the chilly window pane.

When that air hits cold glass, it cools quickly.

Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor.

Extra vapor becomes tiny droplets—fog on the glass.

Wiping clears a peephole; a little fresh air helps too.

Breath on a bathroom mirror makes the same kind of cloud.

Outdoor frost is different—frozen crystals, not indoor steam fog.

Cooking and showers add extra indoor moisture on cold days.

Foggy windows are indoor clouds starting on cold glass.

Open a crack with a grown-up if the room feels too steamy.

Warm moist air, cold pane: window-fog science.

stories.title: Why Do Seasons Feel Different by the Ocean?
stories.text:
Coast feels milder than inland. "Why?" asks Guangguang.

Oceans heat up slowly and cool down slowly.

That big water buffer softens the air nearby.

Coasts often have milder winters than deep inland places.

Summers by the sea can stay cooler than far inland heat.

Breezes carry the ocean’s temperature influence ashore.

Same latitude can still feel different coast versus prairie.

Pack layers for beach trips—wind can still bite.

Foggy marine air is another coastal weather personality.

Oceans are giant temperature shock absorbers for coastal weather.

Compare a seaside day with an inland cousin’s weather report.

Slow ocean buffer: coastal season science.

stories.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
stories.text:
Autumn trees wear red and gold coats.

Green comes from chlorophyll making food.

In fall, many trees slow that green work.

Chlorophyll fades, and other colors show.

Yellows and oranges were hiding underneath.

Some reds form as sugars change in cool air.

Shorter days signal leaves to prepare.

A gentle leaf scar seals where the leaf lets go.

Fallen leaves can feed the soil later.

Not every tree turns the same rainbow.

Fall color is chemistry wearing a costume.

Catch one leaf—then smile at the season.

stories.title: Why Do Volcanoes Erupt?
stories.text:
A mountain with a soft puff sits in a drawing.

Deep Earth can be hot enough to melt rock.

Melted rock is called magma.

Magma can find a path upward through cracks.

When it reaches the surface, we call it lava.

Gas bubbles help push magma up sometimes.

An eruption is Earth letting pressure out.

Some eruptions are gentle; some are stronger.

Scientists watch volcanoes to keep people safe.

Never visit a real volcano without grown-ups and rules.

Volcanoes build new land over long time.

Hot rock, rising paths, careful respect.

stories.title: What Makes an Earthquake?
stories.text:
A storybook floor wiggles softly underfoot.

Earth's outer shell has big pieces called plates.

Plates move very slowly all the time.

Sometimes stuck edges suddenly slip.

That slip sends shaking waves through the ground.

We feel those waves as an earthquake.

Most quakes are small; some are stronger.

Buildings in quake places use special designs.

Drop, cover, and hold on if grown-ups say practice.

Earthquakes are plate motion, not monsters.

Science helps us prepare and stay calmer.

Steady feet, ready plan, soft courage.

stories.title: Why Do Oceans Have Tides?
stories.text:
Beach water creeps up the sand, then back.

The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans.

Water bulges a little toward the Moon.

Another bulge forms on the opposite side too.

As Earth turns, those bulges sweep along shores.

We see high tide and low tide.

The Sun's pull adds a smaller tide effect.

When Sun and Moon line up, tides can be bigger.

Tide pools appear when water goes out.

Check tide times with a grown-up before exploring.

Tides are gravity dancing with spinning Earth.

Wave hello to the Moon's quiet ocean tug.

stories.title: Why Do Flowers Smell Nice?
stories.text:
A garden blossom smells sweet today.

Many flowers make scents to invite helpers.

Bees and butterflies follow smell and color.

Helpers move pollen from flower to flower.

Pollen travel helps plants make seeds.

Pretty smell is a plant's invitation card.

Not every flower smells sweet to people.

Some smells fit beetles or night moths better.

Sniff gently—do not crush the bloom.

Garden perfume is science plus kindness.

Thank the helpers that answer the scent.

Breathe in soft, smile, leave the flower be.

stories.title: Why Do Trees Need Roots?
stories.text:
Max tugs a tiny weed. "Why do trees need roots?"

Roots drink water and minerals from the soil.

They also anchor the tree so wind does not tip it.

Tiny root hairs increase the drinking surface.

Some roots store food for lean seasons.

Fungi can partner with roots to share nutrients.

Deep roots reach moisture; wide roots grab soil.

Cutting big roots can hurt a living tree—ask grown-ups.

Fallen leaves feed the soil that feeds roots.

Roots are the tree’s quiet underground helpers.

Gently feel soil near a tree with a grown-up.

Drink, hold, store: root science.

stories.title: Why Do We Recycle?
stories.text:
Bins labeled paper and plastic. "Why recycle?" asks Mia.

Recycling gives used materials a new job.

It can save energy compared with making everything new.

Less trash in landfills means more room for Earth care.

Clean, dry recyclables help workers sort safely.

Not every item belongs in the blue bin—check labels.

Reuse first: jars, bags, and boxes can live again.

Reduce means buying less waste when you can.

Recycling is teamwork: home, school, and city.

Old stuff → new stuff with less waste.

Sort a small pile with a grown-up tonight.

Reduce, reuse, recycle: Earth care science.

stories.title: Why Do Mountains Form?
stories.text:
Tall peaks on a map. "How do mountains grow?" asks Max.

Earth’s crust is broken into giant moving plates.

When plates push together, rock can fold upward.

Some mountains rise where magma lifts the land.

Others form when blocks of crust tilt and lift.

Rain and ice slowly carve sharp shapes later.

Mountains can take millions of quiet years.

Hiking trails show layers of old rock stories.

Respect steep places—go with grown-ups.

Push, lift, carve: mountain making.

Trace mountain ridges on a soft map together.

High ground: mountain science.

stories.title: What Are Fossils?
stories.text:
A stone leaf print. "Is this a fossil?" asks Mia.

Fossils are traces of ancient life kept in rock.

Bones, shells, footprints, and leaf prints can fossilize.

Mud or sand can bury remains before they vanish.

Minerals slowly replace soft parts over long time.

Fossils teach us who lived before our cities.

Not every cool rock is a fossil—museums help tell.

Never dig protected sites; look with grown-ups.

Drawings and photos record finds kindly.

Old life stories locked in stone.

Visit a fossil exhibit or book with a grown-up.

Stone stories: fossil science.

stories.title: Why Do Rivers Curve?
stories.text:
A winding blue line on the map. "Why curves?"

Water flows downhill, finding easier paths.

Faster water digs the outer bend a little more.

Slower water drops sand on the inner bend.

Over time, dig and drop make bigger loops.

Curves are called meanders by scientists.

Floods can reshape bends after big rains.

Stay back from steep muddy banks—safety first.

Bridges and boats respect the river’s path.

Flow, dig, drop: river curves.

Trace a river’s loops on a map together.

Winding water: river science.

stories.title: What Is Soil Made Of?
stories.text:
Mia digs a little garden hole. "What is soil?"

Soil mixes broken rock, air, water, and living bits.

Tiny creatures and roots keep soil lively.

Dead leaves and bugs become soft dark humus.

Sandy soil drains fast; clay holds water longer.

Healthy soil grows food and flowers.

Compacting soil with heavy steps can hurt roots.

Mulch and compost feed soil gently.

Wash hands after digging—garden manners.

Rock + life + water = growing ground.

Feel sand vs clay with a grown-up.

Dirt treasure: soil science.

stories.title: Why Do We Have Day and Night?
stories.text:
Sun up, then dark. "Why day and night?" asks Max.

Earth spins like a gentle top once a day.

The side facing the Sun gets daylight.

The side turned away rests in night shadow.

Sunrise and sunset are the turning edges.

We do not feel the spin because everything spins with us.

A globe and lamp can show the light half.

Clocks help us meet the day together.

Sleep fits the dark side’s quiet time.

Spin → light half → dark half.

Try a lamp-globe demo with a grown-up.

Day night spin: Earth science.

stories.title: What Causes Caves?
stories.text:
A dark cozy cave picture. "How do caves form?"

Some caves grow where water slowly dissolves rock.

Limestone is a rock that water can nibble for ages.

Cracks widen into tunnels and rooms.

Dripping water can build stone icicles over time.

Lava tubes are caves left by cooled lava rivers.

Sea caves form where waves carve cliffs.

Only explore caves with trained grown-ups.

Lights, helmets, and buddies keep visits safe.

Water + time + rock = cave rooms.

Look at cave photos in a book together.

Underground rooms: cave science.

stories.title: Why Do Glaciers Move?
stories.text:
A slow river of ice. "Do glaciers really move?" asks Max.

Glaciers are thick ice that flows very slowly downhill.

Their own weight makes ice slide and deform a little.

Meltwater at the bottom can help ice slip.

They scrape rock and carry stones like a bulldozer.

When ice melts back, it leaves valleys and lakes.

Climate warmth can speed melting at the edges.

Scientists measure glacier speed with careful tools.

Visit icy places only with trained grown-ups.

Heavy ice + slope = slow motion.

Watch a short glacier video with a grown-up.

Ice river: glacier science.

stories.title: What Is the Water Cycle?
stories.text:
Puddles disappear. "Where does water go?" asks Mia.

Sun warms water into invisible vapor—evaporation.

Vapor rises, cools, and makes cloud droplets.

Clouds can release rain or snow—precipitation.

Water runs into rivers, lakes, and oceans again.

Some soaks into soil as groundwater.

Plants drink and breathe out vapor too.

The same water travels this loop again and again.

We share Earth’s water—use it kindly.

Evaporate, cloud, fall, flow: a cycle.

Trace the loop on a simple drawing together.

Water journey: cycle science.

stories.title: Why Do Some Rocks Sparkle?
stories.text:
A rock twinkles in sun. "Why sparkle?" asks Max.

Some rocks hold shiny mineral crystals.

Flat crystal faces bounce light like tiny mirrors.

Mica flakes can glitter in granite.

Quartz and other minerals can flash too.

Sparkle is light play, not always a gem treasure.

Never taste rocks; wash hands after collecting.

Ask before taking stones from parks.

A hand lens helps you see crystal shapes.

Minerals + light = twinkle.

Compare a dull rock and a shiny one together.

Twinkle stone: mineral science.

stories.title: What Is an Island?
stories.text:
Water all around a land patch. "What’s an island?"

An island is land completely surrounded by water.

Some rise from volcanoes under the sea.

Others are tips of underwater mountains.

River islands form where channels split.

People, plants, and animals can live on islands.

Bridges or boats connect many islands to shore.

Tides can change the wet edges each day.

Protect island shores—they are delicate homes.

Land + water all around = island.

Find an island on a map with a grown-up.

Surrounded land: island science.

stories.title: Why Do Earthquakes Happen?
stories.text:
The floor wiggles in a drill. "Why quakes?" asks Max.

Earth’s plates push, pull, and slide past each other.

Stress builds until rock slips along a fault.

That sudden slip sends shaking waves.

Most quakes are small; some feel stronger.

Buildings can be made to sway more safely.

Drop, cover, and hold on in a practice drill.

Grown-ups make family safety plans.

Aftershocks are smaller follow-up shakes.

Plate slip → shake waves.

Practice a calm drill with a grown-up.

Shake sense: earthquake science.

stories.title: What Are Minerals?
stories.text:
Shiny salt and a pebble. "What are minerals?"

Minerals are natural solid bits with set recipes.

They grow as crystals with ordered insides.

Rocks are often mixtures of several minerals.

Salt, quartz, and gold are mineral examples.

We use minerals in phones, bikes, and buildings.

Hardness and color help scientists tell them apart.

Collecting is fine where rules allow—ask first.

Wash hands after handling outdoor finds.

Recipe + crystal = mineral.

Sort three pebbles by sparkle with a grown-up.

Building blocks: mineral science.

stories.title: Why Do Beaches Have Sand?
stories.text:
Toes in warm sand. "Where does sand come from?"

Waves and weather break rocks into tiny grains.

Rivers carry grains toward the sea.

Shells and coral can become soft pale sand too.

Wind and water sort grains into beaches.

Different rocks make different sand colors.

Dunes can form when wind piles dry sand.

Leave shells where parks ask you to.

Rinse sandy feet before going indoors.

Break, carry, sort: beach sand.

Look at sand grains with a magnifier together.

Tiny rocks: sand science.

stories.title: What Is Compost?
stories.text:
A bin of leaves and peels. "What is compost?"

Compost is food scraps and yard bits broken down.

Tiny helpers—bugs, fungi, microbes—do the work.

Air and a little moisture keep the helpers happy.

Over time scraps become dark crumbly soil food.

Fruit peels yes; meat and oily scraps often no.

Finished compost feeds gardens gently.

Less kitchen trash goes to the landfill.

Wash hands after helping with the bin.

Scraps + helpers = garden gold.

Add a banana peel with a grown-up’s bin rules.

Kitchen to garden: compost science.

stories.title: Why Do Trees Help the Air?
stories.text:
Max breathes under a tree. "How do trees help air?"

Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air.

Using sunlight, they make food for the tree.

They release oxygen that animals and people breathe.

Shade from trees can cool hot sidewalks.

Roots and leaves also catch dust gently.

Forests are big air helpers for the whole planet.

Planting and caring for trees is Earth kindness.

Never carve bark—trees need their skin.

Take in CO2, give out oxygen: leaf work.

Water a young tree with a grown-up.

Fresh breath: tree-air science.

stories.title: What Is Groundwater?
stories.text:
Mia wonders about a well. "What’s groundwater?"

Rain soaks down through soil and rock cracks.

Water collects in underground spaces like a sponge.

That hidden water is called groundwater.

Wells and springs can bring it up carefully.

It moves slowly—much slower than a river.

Clean soil helps keep groundwater healthier.

Don’t dump chemicals outside—ask grown-ups.

Many towns drink groundwater every day.

Rain down → store below → use wisely.

Look at a simple well diagram together.

Hidden water: groundwater science.

stories.title: Why Do We Need National Parks?
stories.text:
A park map with a bear icon. "Why national parks?"

Parks protect wild places for animals and plants.

People can visit to learn, hike, and wonder.

Rules keep trails, nests, and water safer.

Rangers teach and help when visitors need care.

Parks save stories of rocks, trees, and history.

Leave no trash—pack out what you pack in.

Stay on paths so tiny homes stay uncrushed.

Photos are better souvenirs than taking rocks.

Protect + share = park promise.

Plan a park day with a grown-up someday.

Wild classroom: park science.

stories.title: Eyes Get Tired—Time to Rest
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Eyes Get Tired—Time to Rest.

Guangguang: Max, you're staring at that screen like a statue.

Max: One more minute! Just one!

Guangguang: One minute often turns into eleven.

Guangguang: Sore eyes and fewer blinks? That's the alarm.

Max: How do I turn the alarm off?

Guangguang: Stop. Look far away. Soft blink.

Guangguang: Stand up and walk a little bit.

Max: So after this episode I stop?

Guangguang: After this episode—you stop. Say it.

Max: I stop. Then I pass Safety Theater!

Guangguang: Eye care isn't winning or losing—it's care. Rest now.

stories.title: Look Far, Then Near
stories.text:
Mia's nose nearly touches the tablet. "Too close!"

Eyes work hard when everything stays near.

Looking far lets eye muscles change focus.

Near work is fine in short friendly turns.

Then glance out a window to something distant.

Trees, clouds, or a far wall all help.

Far, then near—like a gentle stretch for eyes.

Guangguang coaches: chin up, soft blinks.

If the screen feels sticky-close, scoot back.

Rest breaks protect comfort, not just rules.

Mia practices: far tree, then tablet, smile.

Eyes happy: look far, then come back near.

stories.title: Bright Screens Need Soft Light
stories.text:
A dark room makes the screen feel like a hard spotlight.

Bright screens in black rooms tire eyes faster.

Add a soft lamp behind or beside you.

Room light should be gentle, not a glare fight.

Lower screen brightness until it feels calm.

Max tries: lamp on, brightness down, better.

Avoid watching in a pitch-black cave feeling.

Daytime near a window can be nicely balanced.

If you squint, the light mix needs a tweak.

Soft light + fair screen = kinder eyes.

Guangguang dims the glow and smiles.

Light the room softly—then enjoy the show.

stories.title: Sit Up, Don’t Bend Close
stories.text:
Mia folds like a pretzel over her book.

Bending close makes neck and eyes work harder.

Sit up with soft shoulders and a tall spine.

Bring the book or tablet up—not your nose down.

A pillow or stand can lift the screen kindly.

Feet on the floor help your whole posture.

Short wiggle breaks keep bodies happy.

Guangguang mirrors a proud sitting pose.

If you catch a slump, reset gently—no scolding.

Comfort now means easier reading later.

Sit up, soft eyes, friendly page distance.

Pretzel rest is for snacks—not for screens!

stories.title: Blink and Sip Water
stories.text:
"When did you last blink?" Max wonders.

Screens can make us forget soft blinks.

Blinking spreads a tear film like a tiny wipe.

Dry scratchy eyes often need more blinks.

Sip water—bodies and eyes like gentle sips.

Set a cozy blink-and-sip habit during play.

Look away, blink slowly three times, smile.

Guangguang counts blinks like a game.

If eyes feel sandy, tell a grown-up.

Comfort drinks and blinks are eye kindness.

Max blinks, sips, and the screen feels softer.

Blink, sip, continue—little care, big comfort.

stories.title: Outdoor Light Helps Eyes
stories.text:
Mia steps into soft daylight. "Outdoor light helps eyes?"

Natural light is gentler than staring at one bright screen.

Looking far across a park gives eye muscles a stretch.

A short outdoor break can rest tired near-focus eyes.

Sunglasses help on very bright days—ask a grown-up.

Shade trees and hats can soften strong sun.

Play catch or walk—moving eyes feel happier.

Indoor lamps still help when days are short.

Balance screen time with outdoor looks.

Far light + blinks = kinder eyes.

Take a ten-minute outdoor peek with a grown-up.

Daylight pause: eye-care science.

stories.title: Hot Stove, Cool Hands
stories.text:
A stove glows. "Hot stove—cool hands," says Guangguang.

Burners and pots can stay hot after cooking.

Keep a safe step-back space from the stove.

Only grown-ups turn knobs and move hot pans.

Handles should point inward so sleeves don’t catch.

If something spills hot, call a grown-up—don’t wipe alone.

Oven mitts are for helpers who know how.

Curious sniffing from afar is safer than touching.

A kitchen timer reminds everyone to check safely.

Hot means grown-up zone.

Practice pointing to the stove’s safe line together.

Cool hands: kitchen safety.

stories.title: Knives Are for Grown-Ups
stories.text:
Mia sees a cutting board. "Knives are for grown-ups."

Sharp edges cut food—and can cut skin.

Kids can wash fruit or tear lettuce instead.

Ask before touching any tool in the drawer.

Grown-ups keep knives pointed down and away.

Plastic kid cutters are different—still ask first.

If a knife falls, step back; don’t catch it.

A safe helper job: carry plates with two hands.

Praise careful hands more than fast hands.

Sharp = grown-up tool.

Choose a no-knife helper task together.

Careful kitchen: tool safety.

stories.title: Medicine Is Not Candy
stories.text:
Colorful pills in a bottle. "Not candy," warns Guangguang.

Medicine can look sweet but is measured for bodies.

Only a grown-up or nurse gives the right dose.

Never share medicine with friends.

Closed cabinets keep bottles out of little hands.

If you find a pill on the floor, tell an adult.

Vitamins also need grown-up rules.

Stickers and cartoons on bottles don’t mean treats.

Feeling sick? Describe it; don’t self-dose.

Medicine = grown-up job.

Practice “tell an adult” with a pretend bottle.

Not candy: medicine safety.

stories.title: Don’t Climb on Furniture
stories.text:
Mia eyes a bookshelf. "Don’t climb furniture."

Shelves and dressers can tip if pulled.

Climbing chairs to reach high things can slip.

Ask a grown-up to get the high toy.

Anchored furniture is safer—grown-ups check straps.

Sofas are for sitting, not launching.

Build forts on the floor with pillows instead.

If something wobbles, step away and call help.

Proud feet stay on the floor or playgrounds.

High reach = ask, don’t climb.

Practice asking for the high shelf together.

Steady home: furniture safety.

stories.title: Smoke Alarm Means Go Outside
stories.text:
Beep-beep practice. "Smoke alarm means go outside."

The loud sound is a helper, not a monster.

Leave toys; walk quickly to the meeting place.

Stay low if air feels smoky—grown-ups lead.

Never hide; firefighters look for you outside.

Feel doors with a grown-up before opening.

Call emergency numbers only with an adult plan.

Practice drills make real days calmer.

Batteries in alarms are grown-up check jobs.

Hear beep → go out → stay together.

Walk the family exit path once together.

Alarm helper: fire drill safety.

stories.title: Stop, Look, Listen at Crossings
stories.text:
Curb edge. "Stop, look, listen," says Mia.

Stop at the edge before wheels or feet go.

Look left, right, then left again for cars.

Listen for engines, bells, and horns.

Cross with a grown-up on busy streets.

Make eye contact with drivers when you can.

Phones wait—eyes on the road first.

Rain and dark need extra careful looking.

Bike riders follow the same stop-look-listen.

Pause → eyes → ears → then go.

Practice at a quiet corner with a grown-up.

Street smart: crossing safety.

stories.title: Wait for the Green Light
stories.text:
Traffic light. "Wait for green," says Max.

Red means stop; green means check then go.

Yellow means get ready to stop—don’t rush.

Walk signals show a person or a hand.

Even on green, look both ways once more.

Turning cars may still move—stay alert.

Hold a grown-up’s hand at big lights.

Never dart between parked cars.

Patience keeps toes safer than hurry.

Light color is a shared street language.

Watch one full light cycle together.

Green means go carefully: light safety.

stories.title: Hold a Grown-Up’s Hand
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 14. Hold a Grown-Up’s Hand.

Guangguang: Mia, crossing alone is not a badge of bravery.
Mia: I'm big now!
Guangguang: Big kids still hold a grown-up's hand in busy streets.
Mia: Hand hold = safe?
Guangguang: Hand hold = safe. Together beats lost.
Mia: Hold hand. Cross together.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Bike Helmet On
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 15. Bike Helmet On.

Guangguang: Max, helmet hair is a hero look.
Max: Helmets are hot and silly!
Guangguang: Helmets protect your smart brain if you tip.
Max: So on before wheels roll?
Guangguang: Helmet on, then ride. Click it. Fit it.
Max: Helmet on. Then go.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Stay Where a Grown-Up Can See
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 16. Stay Where a Grown-Up Can See.

Guangguang: Mia, hide-and-seek in a mall is a bad sequel.
Mia: I'll be right back!
Guangguang: Stay where a grown-up can see you.
Mia: In sight—not around the corner?
Guangguang: In sight. If you get separated, find a worker or stay put as you practiced.
Mia: Stay visible.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Strangers Are Not Instant Friends
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 17. Strangers Are Not Instant Friends.

Guangguang: Max, a smile is nice. Instant best-friend? Not always.
Max: He offered candy!
Guangguang: Strangers are not instant friends. Kind can still be unknown.
Max: So I check with my grown-up?
Guangguang: Check first. Don't go. Don't take. Tell a trusted adult.
Max: Not instant friends. Ask first.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Say No and Find a Trusted Adult
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 18. Say No and Find a Trusted Adult.

Guangguang: Mia, what if a plan feels wrong in your tummy?
Mia: Be polite and stay?
Guangguang: You can say no. Then find a trusted adult.
Mia: No is allowed?
Guangguang: No is allowed. Your safety comes first. Practice the words.
Mia: Say no. Find my grown-up.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Passwords Stay Private
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 19. Passwords Stay Private.

Guangguang: Max, is your password a secret or a billboard?
Max: I told my classmate so we can share!
Guangguang: Passwords stay private. Sharing can unlock your stuff for others.
Max: Even friends?
Guangguang: Even friends. Grown-ups help if you forget—not the whole class.
Max: Password private.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Ask Before Clicking Links
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 20. Ask Before Clicking Links.

Guangguang: Mia, that shiny button says FREE PRIZE.
Mia: Tap tap!
Guangguang: Ask before clicking links. Some links are tricks.
Mia: Ask a grown-up first?
Guangguang: Ask first. If it feels rushy or weird, pause.
Mia: No surprise taps. Ask.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Wash Hands Before Eating
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 21. Wash Hands Before Eating.

Guangguang: Max, your hands visited the playground, then the sandwich?
Max: I'm starving!
Guangguang: Wash hands before eating. Soap beats invisible germ hitchhikers.
Max: Soap, rinse, then food?
Guangguang: Soap, rinse, then food. Quick and powerful.
Max: Wash first. Eat second.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Swim Only With a Grown-Up
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 22. Swim Only With a Grown-Up.

Guangguang: Mia, water is fun—and deep.
Mia: I can doggy-paddle!
Guangguang: Swim only with a grown-up watching. Water rules are not optional.
Mia: No solo swimming?
Guangguang: No solo. Grown-up eyes on. Life jackets when they say so.
Mia: Grown-up with me.
Guangguang: Pass.

stories.title: Wear Sunscreen Outside
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 23. Wear Sunscreen Outside.

Guangguang: Max, the sun is strong even when you feel fine.
Max: Sunscreen is sticky!
Guangguang: Wear sunscreen outside. Sticky now beats burn later.
Max: Put it on before play?
Guangguang: Before play. Grown-ups help with face and ears.
Max: Sunscreen on. Then run.
Guangguang: Pass Safety Theater.

stories.title: Tell an Adult If Something Hurts
stories.text:
Please listen. Guangguang Safety Theater. Episode 24. Tell an Adult If Something Hurts.

Guangguang: Mia, brave is not silent when something hurts.
Mia: I don't want to bother anyone.
Guangguang: Tell an adult if something hurts—body or feelings.
Mia: Saying it is okay?
Guangguang: Saying it helps them help you. Early words beat big worries.
Mia: If it hurts, I tell.
Guangguang: Pass. You're Safety Theater strong.
